Good morning.

For the third time in a matter of weeks, EU ambassadors will try on Friday (6 November) to agree whether to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year or by three.

Big Oil, the Trump administration and a growing group of member states have been pushing for a delay, citing supply and legal risks.

For a long time the commission refused <https://email.mgeu.euobserver.com/c/eJyEkc1unzAQxJ_G3BzhDww-cKj0F6-BjL2AG_whe502b1-RpmlTVep1d2dm9ZvNoD1X72Yl-dDZFBG-4wwtbRXKCxTqjL9en7gcRS87Nw8W1NjBzEYttFRKj90590KCHOzIFdPDPvRcCs6mXYqdGT5trPNzgZDXYPwFZWVy2iSTcv0wUUT24YD29Dv4yabQfU3bz9_Y1F3ziZgrEV8IXwhfPp8SvnAup0ERvuAJBSo19EpI006zid4--3hQs6WGFBoNgKeJQEu7oNKtIXWJHqbS2nK-XimeBQxWapyjLd-BYikYVnt5-0zEQ2sGTo6acHWPa2rFAhGPv8G97wM438K9vxG8D60J2fgjfpKtIZXo47G27AzC2ivGuPqluOuJSMTjra3ba60QHZSb0jBpPWqxf1AdujJH-FYvQITCpBCayP64ZW90_-z537kdQsiXQfj_5cvMfwQAAP__4e3EBQ> to propose a delay, but in October it finally buckled and proposed one year.

🗞️ Cars are stupid. Throw rocks at them!

6 November 2026 | Daily newsletter

͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌

Good morning,

I rarely feel the impact of whatever my political representatives sit around doing all day. But one thing would change my life immediately: wider, safer bike lanes, and more of them. Cycling in most European cities feels like an obstacle course where you either arrive drenched in sweat with lungs full of car exhaust, or you never arrive, because you're literally dead. I. Hate. It. Good thing our correspondents got together to map a more bike-friendly continent for this week's long read.

Toyah Höher

Editor

Cycling

What it takes to get Europe on a bike

Cycling is cheap, healthy, and convenient. So why don’t more Europeans do it?

〉 Read article 〉 Hide again

Belle de Jong, Ludovica Di Meco, Liene Lūsīte, Tamara Kaňuchová, Toon Vos

On 22 September in Turin, Italy, a car hit and killed a seven-year-old boy cycling to school. “That could have been me, or my daughter, or anyone, really. Because that place is dangerous,” resident Maria Cristina Caimotto told us.

Every morning since then, Caimotto has joined a crowd of people on bikes in the street where the tragedy took place to show solidarity with the family, but also to ask for safer streets and fewer cars. “We cannot erase what happened. We can only do everything we can so that it does not happen again,” she said.

Backed by 13 civil society associations, the activists want Turin to move away from its dependence on cars.

It’s ambitious, but not impossible: a similar tragedy helped push the Netherlands to become the cycling country it is today.

Until the 1970s, the Netherlands was full of cars. In 1971, a six-year-old was killed cycling to school, and her father's newspaper article launched the “Stop de Kindermoord” (Stop the Child Murder) campaign against children dying in traffic.

Two years later, the oil crisis added fuel to the fire, driving up petrol prices, and in 1977, Groningen became the first city in the Netherlands with a plan prioritising cyclists over cars.

Nowadays, 82% of Dutch residents cycle at least occasionally and the country has more than 24 million bikes for a population of about 18 million people. Utrecht now tops the Copenhagenize Index, which ranks the world’s most bicycle-friendly cities, and Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and The Hague are in the top 30.

The Dutch protests worked because they were about more than getting around, says Meredith Glaser, professor of cycling at Ghent University and CEO of the Urban Cycling Institute: “These protests weren’t about transportation. They were about the security of our children, the liveability of our cities, how inclusive they are.”

I want to ride my bicycle

Italy is taking small steps in the same direction: bike paths increased by 28.8% between 2019 and 2024, Milan presented new walking and cycling guidelines last April, and Rome plans to add 185 km to its network in the next three years.

In Riga, the Latvian capital, the bike path network has nearly doubled since 2020, from 98 km to around 190 km today, according to Oto Ozols, deputy head of the municipality’s cycling infrastructure division. And people are using it, even in winter. “As many people were cycling in summer 10 years ago as are cycling in winter now,” said Ozols.

For inspiration, Riga looked to Helsinki, Copenhagen, and Dutch cities. All rank high in the Copenhagenize Index, which Europe dominates: 27 of its top 30 cities in 2025 were European.

The columns contain the following countries. Iberia: Spain, Portugal; Balkans, Greece & Cyprus: Slovenia, Croatia, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Cyprus; Central Europe: Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary; Nordics & Baltics: Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania; Benelux: Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg.

Windows of opportunity

You don’t have to be a big city to make cycling work. In Malacky, a town of around 19,000 people in Slovakia, 11 km of cycling lanes and an additional network of roads shared with cars (which usually come with a low speed limit) have already turned the bike into an everyday mode of transport.

Zuzana, who lives there, said: “The traffic jams are so bad that we can’t even get onto the highway to leave town. So if I need to get around town, the bike is the ideal choice for me.” For her, the reasons add up: “Fuel here costs two euros now [per litre], it hits the wallet. The fact that we’re saving the environment is a huge plus. And health, of course. We’re getting some exercise.”

She got into cycling during the Covid-19 pandemic, exploring the regional cycling routes connected to her town. During the pandemic, cycling offered an alternative to both public transport and the gym. In Paris, lockdowns had a similar effect: an existing bike plan for the Rue de Rivoli was rolled out almost overnight.

Between 2021 and 2027, the EU dedicated €4.5 billion to cycling projects, significantly more than in the 2014-2020 period. Grants for projects are often tied specifically to cycling lanes, so the allocated money cannot be used for anything else.

Malacky had approved cycling plans back in 2015, so it was ready when EU funding calls appeared. It also invested from its own budget in street lighting and green strips separating the bike lanes from traffic, because cycling infrastructure only works if the space around it does too.

Ozols says EU funding helped in Riga, too, by requiring the city to cooperate with neighbouring municipalities so routes don’t stop at the city limits.

Ruth Oldenziel, a technology historian at Eindhoven University of Technology who leads the Cycling Cities research project, says moments like the pandemic and EU funding calls are “windows of opportunity” worth preparing for. “You can think about which types of knowledge and policy you can already put in place so that when that moment of opportunity arises, you are ready.”

How we lost the bike

Between 1890 and 1920, people cycled in cities all over the world, Oldenziel explained. Over the 20th century, streets were handed over to cars – in the Netherlands, too. What set the Dutch apart, Oldenziel said, is that cycling lobbies and unions never let the bike drop off the political agenda. “It’s not that the Netherlands invented cycling, but we kept cycling.”

Riga shows what happens when a city doesn’t.

In the 1930s, it was cycle-friendly: on a single day in June 1937, nearly 6,000 cyclists crossed the pontoon bridge over the Daugava, according to newspaper clippings Ozols shared with us. Between 1920 and 1941, the number of bicycles in the city grew from around 1,200 to over 42,000. That's roughly one bicycle for every ten residents in 1941.

Under Soviet rule, however, streets were widened and entire blocks demolished to make room for cars – all in pursuit of a modern city. “The Soviets copied the Americans: highways, wide streets, and so on,” Ozols told us. Soviet authorities even banned cycling on several streets, including Brīvības Street, one of Riga's main arteries.

“What we see in the 20th century is a transformation of the street, from a place where children played, where people met, where there were shops – a very social space – into what we call traffic: corridors for cars, corridors for pedestrians, all corridors,” Oldenziel explained.

Who gets the street?

Across the EU, the car still stands strong: there were 584 passenger cars per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, and the fleet grew by 6.5% between 2020 and 2025, with some of the fastest growth in central and eastern member states such as Romania, Croatia, and Lithuania.

Italy has 709 cars per 1,000 residents, the EU’s highest rate. Its public transport also reaches fewer places than the EU average, leaving small towns and southern regions especially disconnected. It is not a surprise that two-thirds of daily trips in Italy are made by car.

According to Luigi Menna, president of the Italian Federation for the Environment and Cycling (FIAB), “there's too much bureaucracy, and the political world can be short-sighted, especially since the ownership and use of private cars generates considerable revenue in taxes.”

There's also a psychological aspect: “People fear that cycling will take away parking spaces from cars, and this hinders the development of new infrastructure,” Menna added.

In car-centred Riga, every lost car lane triggers heated debate in Facebook comment sections. But Helsinki, one of Riga's models and sixth in the Copenhagenize Index, is facing the same backlash. “The comments look exactly like the ones in Riga,” Ozols said. Residents tend to come round, he argues, because the lanes come with trees, benches, and drinking fountains. “They improve public space and pedestrian safety,” he said.

Without safe cycling routes, cyclists avoiding traffic end up on the pavement with pedestrians, squeezed into the same leftover space while cars keep theirs. In city centres, Oldenziel said, “shared space is actually much better, but it only works if motorists are guests.”

For Ozols, the goal is “safe mobility from eight to eighty”: a network that both children and older people can use. “Once people feel safe cycling on the road with a child, cyclists will stop riding on pavements,” he explained. “They don’t ride on the pavement because it’s faster – it’s always faster to cycle on the road – but simply because they’re afraid.”

Networks, not lanes

A safe bike lane only helps if it leads somewhere, and the destination is often a bus or train station. “You might focus your cycle paths largely on getting everyone to the train station,” explained Dan Kollár, president of Cyklokoalícia, Slovakia’s biggest NGO advocating for sustainable mobility. Railway stations in many of Slovakia's larger cities are “neither comfortable nor safe to access by bicycle”, he said.

Riga is doing just that by developing mobility hubs around railway stations. “There’s bicycle parking, space for shared cars, and public transport connections that make it easy to get off and transfer to a train, and vice versa,” Ozols explained. “Our planned cycle routes link all those railway stations together like beads on a string.”

“The key to healthy urban mobility is variety, because people will use different modes and combine them,” Ozols said. Making alternatives attractive, he argues, benefits people who continue to drive, too. “The aim shouldn’t be that nobody drives, but simply that people drive less in their everyday lives.”

A recipe for success

So what's the full recipe for a cycling city?

Start with the shape of the city: its density, geography, and existing infrastructure, and design cycling infrastructure around it. Check the alternatives: does public transport work with the bike, or replace it? Add policy that makes room for cycling instead of steering money towards cars.

Stir in people pushing for change, as in Italy and the Netherlands. And finally, season with positive public perception of bikes: as a sign of a green lifestyle rather than poverty, as a sport, or simply as a practical way to get around.

Once you have the ingredients, someone still needs to cook – and that’s where it often goes wrong, according to Kollár: “When bike lanes are built, it is often simply because EU funds happened to be available, or because people argued for them, rather than because the decision-makers truly viewed cycling as a genuine solution.”

Where that belief exists, though, change can come fast: “When there are politicians in place that have a vision and have the capacity and competencies […] then we can see change happening rather quickly,” said Glaser. Malacky and Riga are proof: one had its plans ready before the money came, the other nearly doubled its network in six years.

So can any place become a cycling city? Oldenziel thinks so, pointing to her own city in the 1970s: “When I was growing up, Amsterdam was terrible for cycling. It was dangerous,” she said. “Any city can become a Dutch cycling city, but you have to stick with it. [...] You need a vision and a master plan. And you simply have to keep pushing for that change.”

In Turin, Caimotto and her neighbours are doing exactly that.

The Russian Vikings

A History of Mankind (419)

David Roman

Nov 6

Preview

READ IN APP

Norsemen were dominated by the idea of fate.

For centuries in the middle of the 1st millennium, they had seen a colder climate destroy crops and drive many to join the Great Migrations down on the continent that eventually overwhelmed much of the Roman Empire. Moreover, they were displaced from some of their ancient areas of settlement by the arrivals of newcomers better suited to the new climate.

As Sami nomads long accustomed to the freezing cold of northern Scandinavia and their former Uralic homeland moved southwards¹ with their domesticated reindeer and settled in the wastes of modern Finland (which they called Suomi), the Norwegian population crowded around fishing regions along the western shore and the relatively warmer Oslo Fjord.

In other places, the consequences were even more dire: many regions of central Sweden were almost completely abandoned, with woodland growing over empty fields, and well over a thousand farms were left vacant in the Baltic islands of Gotland – the mythic land of the Goths – and Oland/Oeland. Across Scandinavia temperatures fell by at least two degrees, and possibly as many as three to four. In Norway, where only three percent of the land is suitable for farming as of the 21st century…

“… this would have been enough to render significant parts of the country uninhabitable through the collapse of viable cereal cultivation. The regression of woodland into what had once been food-producing fields shows that, in many places, agriculture itself had ceased. Acid rain caused by the eruptions may even have affected marine life, including fish catches, although to a lesser degree than the agricultural catastrophe. The worst of these effects went on for three years. In 2016 a team of climate scientists suggested that the long-term, cumulative ecological impact of the dust veil persisted in varying degrees for up to eighty years.”²

The Svear, people of southern Sweden who eventually had the whole country named after them “(Sverige” in Swedish) only managed to hold on to their land with the help of trade with Denmark and, as in Norway, extensive fishing.

Credit: Historymaps.com...

Handler in New York: Ist es KI-Panik oder Demokraten-Panik? (Foto: AFP)

Guten Morgen, liebe Leserin, lieber Leser, für die politische Kultur mag der Sieg der Demokraten bei den US-Zwischenwahlen ein Segen sein – für die wirtschaftlichen Aussichten gilt das nicht ganz so bedingungslos. Und das spürt zuerst der Tech-Sektor. Keine Branche ist ein so enges Bündnis mit Donald Trump eingegangen wie diese, keine hat so profitiert wie die Tech- und KI-Firmen – und keine andere Branche steht nun so unter Druck. Die Aktien borsennotierter Tech-Unternehmen gaben gestern in den USA auf breiter Front nach.

Der Index der Technologieborse Nasdaq rauschte um 5,5 Prozent ins Minus, der Dow Jones um 3,4 Prozent, der marktbreite S&P 500 um 4,4 Prozent. Vor allem Chiphersteller verloren, Nvidia etwa gut neun Prozent, und gab damit alle Gewinne des Jahres wieder ab.

Es scheint, als litten die Aktienmarkte unter Trump-Entwohnung – und der Furcht, dass die Demokraten den Ausbau der Infrastruktur für KI deutlich bremsen und die KI-Entwicklung starker regulieren konnten. Allerdings versteckten sich auch weitere Gründe für den gestrigen Borsenabsturz hinter den plakativen Wahlergebnissen: So enttauschten die Ausblicke der Chiphersteller Qualcomm und Arm. Und für das Analysehaus Kobeissi sind die Kursverluste auch Ergebnis kreditfinanzierter Wetten:

Genau das passiert, wenn die Stimmung in einem überhebelten Markt kippt.

Und doch zeigen die Borsenturbulenzen eben auch: Der Triumph der Trump-Bezwinger ist keine sichere Erfolgsgeschichte. Vor allem wirtschaftlich dürfte der politische Wechsel noch Nebenwirkungen haben. Im Kleinen werden etwa deutsche Unternehmen mit Investitionsplanen in den USA merken, dass der industriefreundliche Wind der vergangenen Jahre sich dreht. Im Großen konnte die deutlichste Schnittmenge zwischen Trump und linken Demokraten darin bestehen, die Staatsverschuldung immer weiter hochzuschrauben – und damit auch die Instabilitat, die schon jetzt vom US-Schuldenberg für die internationalen Markte ausgeht.

Dass Trump in seiner Macht eingeschrankt wird, ist natürlich für die Welt ein Signal der Hoffnung – ein Garant für ein sorgloses Leben ist es nicht.

USA: Das neue Amerika

Für die Demokratie gut, aber womoglich nicht für die Wirtschaft – genau dieses „Ja, aber“ bringt den Digitalunternehmer Philipp Depiereux auf. Der Deutsche, der teilweise in Kalifornien lebt, schrieb mir nach der Wahl:

Die Midterms haben gezeigt, dass die amerikanische Demokratie wehrhaft ist. Deutschland reagiert darauf mit Bedenken. Das sagt mehr über uns als über die USA.

Er glaubt, dass mit dem Wahlergebnis das Ende der Ara Trump beginnt:

Untersuchungsausschüsse, Vorladungen, das Haushaltsrecht: Der Prasident wird nicht mehr durchregieren konnen.

Und dass Deutschland davon lernen kann:

Das dürfen wir feiern, ohne naiv zu sein. Und wir sollten uns davon etwas abschauen, bevor wir selbst erleben müssen, wie schnell Institutionen unter Druck geraten.

Darin ist sich Depiereux einig mit dem Autorenteam unserer dieswochigen Titelgeschichte: Auch das hat ein neues Amerika entdeckt und beschreibt die Chancen, die aus der neuen Lage in den USA entstehen. Ein paar „Aber“ haben sie, Depiereux wird es verzeihen, auch eingefügt.

In Frankreich kam es gestern bei landesweiten Streiks und Protesten erneut zu Krawallen. Schwappt die Jugendrevolte dauerhaft nach Deutschland? Der Berliner Soziologe Steffen Mau glaubt das nicht, wie er meinem Kollegen Dietmar Neuerer und mir gesagt hat. Beruhigend ist seine Diagnose trotzdem nicht: Er erlebe „einen erheblichen Fruststau“ im Land.

Das ist insofern bemerkenswert, als Mau bisher eher als Optimist unter den Sozialforschern galt. Nun sagt er: „Mich überrascht, wie schnell die Verschiebungen gehen.“ Die Bundesregierung beherrsche ihr Handwerk nicht, betreibe „Politik im Flackermodus“ und bevorzuge ohnehin die Generation 50 plus. Die Folge: Es gebe „die Vorstellung eines kollektiven Fahrstuhls nach unten“.

Walberg: „Aufgeben ist keine Option.“ (Foto: Walberg Urban Electrics)

E-Roller: Der Mann hinter dem Boom

In Hamburg betreibt Florian Walberg mit Egret den wohl letzten deutschen E-Scooter-Hersteller von Belang. Also Exot in einem boomenden Markt: Die Zahl privater E-Scooter stieg von 571.000 im Jahr 2022 auf zuletzt 1,36 Millionen. Die meisten verkaufen die chinesischen Hersteller Xiaomi und Segway, Egret kommt auf 3,8 Prozent.

„Engineered in Germany“, gebaut in China – das ist Walbergs Geschaftsmodell und zugleich sein Dilemma. Warum er keine Alternative sieht, erklart er meiner Kollegin Annika Keilen an einem einzigen Bauteil: Für den Controller verlangte ein süddeutscher Zulieferer 750.000 Euro Entwicklungsgeld vorab, zwei Jahre Zeit und 150 bis 200 Euro pro Stück. In China kostet ein vergleichbares Teil 30 bis 40 Dollar, fertig in zwei Monaten. Seinen Ausweg sucht Walberg im Fachhandel, wo er acht Prozent Umsatz, aber 50 Prozent seines Gewinns macht. Dass Segway nun auch dorthin drangt, nimmt er sportlich:

Wir müssen nur mitschwimmen und sie nicht besiegen.

Eine Durchhaltestrategie, die seinem Heimatstandort nicht ganz fremd ist.

Heinz Ketchup: Marktführer mit Milliardenverlust. (Foto: Kraft Heinz/PR (2), Getty Images [M])

Ketchup: Die Abnehmspritze, die die Gewinne ausdünnt

Zum Schluss schauen wir auf eine Marke, die seit 1999 sogar auf der Raumstation ISS verzehrt wird: Heinz Ketchup ist Weltmarktführer, der Mutterkonzern Kraft Heinz schrieb 2025 trotzdem 5,85 Milliarden Dollar Verlust. Und die großte Bewahrungsprobe steht erst noch bevor: die Massenverbreitung von Ozempic und Co. Jeder fünfte US-Amerikaner hat bereits Abnehmspritzen oder -pillen genutzt, die den Appetit auf Süßes und Fettiges dampfen.

Heinz-Europachef Willem Brandt sieht das allerdings gar nicht so negativ. Er erhofft sich sogar Wachstumschancen durch Ozempic und Co. Nutzer von Abnehmspritzen nahmen zwar weniger Kalorien, aber deutlich mehr Proteine zu sich. Brandt sagt:

Mageres Fischfilet oder Huhn schmecken nach nichts. Sie brauchen eine geschmackliche Aufwertung – und die bringen unsere Remouladen, Saucen und neuen Ketchup-Varianten.

Ob die Gleichung mit den weniger Kalorien dann noch aufgeht, steht auf einem anderen Blatt.

Hello. Forty-one years ago this week, two French secret service agents pleaded guilty to arson and manslaughter following the bombing of a Greenpeace ship in New Zealand on 10 July 1985. Discover more about the highly controversial state-sponsored sabotage operation below. Also in this edition is a look at how a Russian stray dog became a tragic national hero. Plus, as the UK marks Guy Fawkes Night this evening, we dive into the history of Bonfire Night and why one English region has an "almost cult-like" approach to the celebrations. Happy reading!

VIDEO FROM THE ARCHIVE

'An icon of Soviet space exploration'

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABuNw0BDWKgCew7NvJsmudl2mH8P2xi6uF5akF_VCsFnOPIpvGCjnQLpszsUW26Sy_wRqofPBtTyiLqvrpftzidymChzmoh3db5r7ww In November 1957, Soviet scientists sent Laika on a one-way voyage, making her a tragic national hero. Credit: Alamy

On 3 November 1957, a female stray dog called Laika was launched from Russia's Baikonur Cosmodrome spaceport in Kazakhstan, becoming the first living creature to orbit the Earth.

Between 1951 and 1965, the Soviets sent more than 50 dogs into space, with the flights before Laika being sub-orbital. By choosing dogs for their flights, the Soviets differed from American scientists, who had sent first fruit flies and then monkeys into space.

Sadly, though, Laika did not survive her voyage - and the Soviets knew all along that it would be a one-way trip. "Scientists then did not know how to return living creatures from orbit back to Earth," Prof Viktor Yazdovsky told the BBC's Witness History in 2017. "Everyone was very concerned for Laika. They knew that she would not return from her journey."

Via the button below, learn more about how Laika became an icon of early Soviet space exploration and how her death sparked international outrage, changing the way space programmes handled animal subjects forever.

FIRST DRAFT OF HISTORY

Guilty pleas in Rainbow Warrior trial

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABuNw0BDd8D7_9Cv5CsgCxdYeTRM1mxYDsRObt5Fjmk4NwhG0mas-VOYOHb-EoHKBnAMIEhirL3mMOnrINuXPedzKRS_WFMwmSmckfQ Greenpeace's Rainbow Warrior ship which was bombed and sunk in Auckland Harbour, New Zealand, in July 1985. Credit: Alamy

On this week in 1985, two French secret service agents pleaded guilty to arson and manslaughter relating to the bombing of the Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, New Zealand.

The Greenpeace ship was struck on 10 July 1985, killing Fernando Pereira - a photographer who was on board. Docked in Auckland Harbour, the vessel was preparing to protest against French nuclear testing in the Pacific when it was bombed.

On 3 November 1985, 41 years ago this week, Alain Mafart and Dominique Prieur pleaded guilty to arson and manslaughter.

"The two... admitted manslaughter after charges of murder against them were dropped," reported the BBC at the time - as shown in the script below. "The New Zealand Prime Minister, Mr David Lange, has denied that his government was involved in the decision to drop the murder charges."

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABuNw0BDeLW2dmmHr072N5F0TT03fUTWdQjWVYopHSh5tBdayUV3j3jQpKCUb-QpzcTLTtp0-3LEfqdTwcMxKpYM3bJ_agGOFjHr08g

WHAT HAPPENED NEXT

Compensation and an apology

Mafart and Prieur were sentenced to 10 years in prison for manslaughter and seven years for arson, however a settlement meant they were transferred to a base in French Polynesia and released by 1988.

In the years since, France has apologised and paid damages for the bombing - compensation that funded Greenpeace's replacement of the Rainbow Warrior with a ship of the same name. In 1996, it stopped the nuclear testing that initiated the Greenpeace protest.

In 2015, the French intelligence agent who led the deadly attack in 1985 apologised for his actions for the first time https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABuNw0BDf8VUNdA_YLXrlzivBHuj27hK0pKV2PUiTjGQTIh90zAd7cfboalty9-jx2JVad2Y2uGV1upiXDLhGDu0nx5RKIjgkVAEGeA . Jean-Luc Kister told New Zealand's TVNZ station that it was not the aim of his team to kill anybody and that he wanted to say sorry to Pereira's family.

He said the destruction of the vessel was "disproportionate" and "an unfair, clandestine operation conducted in an allied, friendly and peaceful country".

"We had to obey orders, we were soldiers," he added.

Reader memories

Thanks to everyone who wrote to me in response to last week's email, to share your memories of both the Cuban missile crisis... and Winnie-the-Pooh https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABuNw0BDgLuC66UFWgU-50AJ40GEeQr0a_66pQhGLjnF9rLHJUbhs2RuZRVIpGd_3wy4GepkhMJ1YYMb3BKVvL8dN6F8NY76MZfwEQA

I enjoyed this contribution from Susan Watson in Montreal, Quebec, Canada: "I'm now 65, but I remember fondly getting all the stuffed animals one Christmas when I was little - Winnie-the-Pooh, Kanga and Roo, Piglet, Eeyore, etc. We had the books and we listened to them on my dad's reel-to-reel stereo. My mum made the animals. Kanga and Roo survived into the 2000s and were given to my brother's boy."

And Lynda Smith in Melbourne, Australia, wrote: "I still have my treasured Winnie-the-Pooh set of four books given to me in 1949 by my great-grandmother. They have yellowed with age, but the happy memories of Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore and Tigger etc will never fade."

Do you remember hearing about the bombing of the Rainbow Warrior? Or perhaps you remember Laika's space voyage?

And finally...

Every year on 5 November, people across the UK celebrate Bonfire Night with fireworks, bonfires, sparklers and apples coated in toffee. The date marks the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot - a failed attempt to blow up the Houses of Parliament in 1605. But in one part of England, the festivities are about far more than one night. Revenge of the (Democratic Budget) Nerds

Trump’s rogue OMB director is about to get his wings clipped.

Catherine Rampell • FREE PREVIEW

READ TO ME

Hi everyone, and welcome to this week’s edition of Receipts.

Most Americans couldn’t pick Russell Vought out of a lineup. But the White House budget director has quietly done more to elevate Donald Trump as king than any other cabinet member. This week’s newsletter explains how he did it, and how a new Congress under Democratic control could hold him accountable.

Supporters of democracy are rightly celebrating this week, but there’s lots of work ahead to rebuild the institutions Trump has trampled. That project is at the heart of The Bulwark’s mission, and we’d love to have you alongside us. Get 20% off for 1 year

–Catherine

(Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock)

CONGRESSIONAL DEMOCRATS OBVIOUSLY have lots of things on their to-do list for next year, starting with cost-of-living issues and cracking down on corruption. But there’s another key priority that has gotten less attention but is no less important: restoring the constitutional separation of powers so that Congress actually controls the power of the purse again.

Or to put it in more colorful terms: Congress is about to reclaim its cojones, and then go after the low-profile cabinet member who sliced them off in the first place.

I’m referring to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought. He served in that role for the second half of Trump’s first term, then spent the next four years preparing for a return to office—starting a Trumpian think tank and writing a critical chapter in Project 2025. Since resuming the OMB job, Vought has orchestrated many of Trump’s most brazenly authoritarian moves as president. There’s a reason Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.), the incoming chair of the House Budget Committee, called Vought “the most dangerous man in America that most Americans have never heard of.”

“It’s easy to pay attention to fools like RFK and Hegseth,” says David A. Super, an administrative and constitutional law professor at Georgetown. “But Russ Vought is actually pretty good at his job. He’s just evil as hell.”

Vought is not a clown. And he’s not overtly corrupt. He’s just really, really good at turning Trump into a king.

So let’s talk about some of the sneakiest, most devious ways the Trump administration has been shredding the Constitution, and what the new Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill can do to glue it back together—and maybe inflict a little pain on the guy with the shredder, too.

This gets a bit wonky, but stick with me. I promise it’s worth it.

Of the many jobs AI is creating, I think some of the most interesting are engineers being embedded in other functions (like marketing, HR, finance, and so on) to create workflow automations and help them take advantage of AI.

It is beneficial for everyone — not just developers — to learn to build (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3prW6dQFkn2ntBwxW5kkQRz1NhHznW3p_pF32ttHLJW7DNvgT8_mXtGW5vFwJj5WwH6fW4nKsLH6R8jnhN3B7WYw7FgyVN8Ffh8fPx4lSW1ThStx2DpsBGW4LqnNS8D01d2W60FRfR2w7n8lN4lr_NhQT2XdW5dK7Ll2m2mslW8hk7D42-bmw4VgWRfq6Q3YqxW1kVCZ79lF7bBW6JpBJx2XjS-hW8JjhFg5l0zGhW100SMY8D3xdSW7hbwPy27Cv50W4Z1Mj-5fkykzW9kt1Sg7cZ_JNN54nWgYXmvrcW8B3my03-kbD8W4lwk4-8qwT2zW7d669p1Y5q_Hf3TYMv-04 ) software applications with AI assistance. Still, a developer with AI Engineering skills can do a lot that someone without those skills cannot. Before coding agents, some teams occasionally embedded an engineer in, say, a marketing team. But engineering productivity was lower, and one engineer’s ability to move the needle was limited. Now that AI Engineering has made developers more productive, embedding an engineer in some other function makes much more sense.

For example, AI-savvy engineers can help other teams:

- Implement workflow automations - Create dashboards, perform data analysis, and present insights - Build data infrastructure - Build custom applications (or help buy and integrate third-party ones) - Learn AI engineering and AI usage so that they can do more for themselves

Some of my teams have embedded AI engineers in marketing, recruiting, finance, and other departments. It’s always interesting for engineers to learn about other functions, and those other teams end up with not just better systems but also significantly improved knowledge of AI. In addition, the number of ideas they end up wanting to build always outstrips the capacity of the embedded engineers (because the bottleneck is not coding, but product management, workflow redesign, and other tasks such as judgement tasks (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fx3prCCW95jsWP6lZ3myW7FLPwy2Dw7vCW2SSRbQ93dC4VVyySfH435NXCW22sgxk5H7HX5N7ZKN2WgTw_0W1n3H5q5G04D4W39vMrn8gGV6SW1NbzXZ6YsMflW2KpgTv34dLt0W6QSQHR3_6kD_W1gYFH99hHzF4N2VMZt9jVL6VW4DrzBg23S2cvVwSxp95_LM6BW1TtTwC2g6q7CW1NYg7D7S6scmW7znyy042p8hgN4sl2KygTY1sW72qzj076f6NLW35YrH75R-4GdW26XNr26XWGn-W4MFzN94wlFQWW3jfrbH1hD7KSW4QFzwc1_G0rWVYqrH14fvtstW8Tm0gJ8mnczYW52bRmD9b3wwjW4p_XKL3xS9FzW3nQc851N74GKVcdv-l1QbqPpf7TfHQK04 ) , which still take a significant amount of human effort).

News

Gemini Leads the Pack Again

Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon puts the company on top of Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, edging past Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, while costing less per task. As with Gemini 4 Argon, Google is making Carbon available to select cybersecurity companies ahead of general availability.

What’s new: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fx3prCCW95jsWP6lZ3pRW4M9Hz86Xm2fDV5wq3K5FKlcGW7jnT4v5_nM_NW9lgfhP8_YYhGW7GTHfV5ZrPN2W7bs-d16p-g7nW5fdFvS2V03qnW7WPZvZ8CKMSGW6vd5ph58t_0nN7lDSLvTPMhkW8WmGrP5S4wY8W2Fy-qM60Sgt7M5MZ9CMlnmSW2-xYqB5fvYWhMDxwKn2dgZzW34RXzx41P7_rW8lKVhX2VX48CW7wDP4m6ST8SbV6nS7-3PFWJJW87jmRQ1_8hqkW2l30cG5zLPL1N6Q7JCcxbqG2N8VrSJTXRthhW1LtZlh2w6w_tN5LC_2s8WG2zW7JRmD-35sXRgN7qYhTKlZf00W1phpKl9k1wWkW3XwPTb51GQKtW2QN4Tn60q1dJf6pYytK04 ) , a multimodal model that it says is designed for cybersecurity tasks. There is no set date for Carbon’s wider release.

- Input/output: Text, image, speech, and video in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (94.6 tokens per second) - Features: Adjustable reasoning - Performance: First on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0 (59), second on Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2 (70.36 percent), first on Arena.ai’s Text leaderboard (1,528 Elo) - Availability: A small set of Google-selected companies, with access expanding gradually to other companies in its Fairwind Program - Price: Via API at an introductory price of $2/$0.10/$10 per million input/cached/output tokens, then $4/$0.20/$20 per million input/cached/output tokens - Weights/license: Proprietary - Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods, knowledge cutoff, end date of introductory pricing, date for broader availability

How it works: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3ngV1nh4S6G4-yxV4V0tg9dxQpqN930xRhMnmfNW4GWj6T7R9bQKV-XDhg4GPlLSW7ZVV9n1fgSG0W7J6j694xBJtDW4SQbyh2g-jnsW18Txfp5WN0KHN1lQV4gGtJLwW3dkk-b2fHPvpW8z2pQ-4NQwhKW3Pl22652C_h7VLT3qb8xY6swW7_qk-s7tdc-yW4DHHvn1QbkVKW67gpvC7XXP6mN8J8kj6xGymxW8YTCkt6d32bXW3j7wKk1YPz5wW1ck1pM19L-vWW3N2-WC3c5HmFVsW7T12SGx0wW8zYbvd69cQp2W1qZzvn5txsHJW2PN6p142nlBYf5M0RM004 ) , which it described as a mixture-of-experts model trained via reinforcement learning on reasoning, problem-solving, and theorem-proving data. The company says it worked to improve Carbon in coding, science, multistep agentic tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Carbon shares Gemini 4 Argon’s safety measures, including resistance to prompt injection and adversarial prompts. The company also filtered Argon and Carbon’s training data to remove sexual abuse material, personally identifiable information, and pages from low-trust websites.

Performance: Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first on Artificial Analysis’ recently updated Intelligence Index v5.0 and second on Vals AI’s Vals Index. It leads most tests of expert knowledge and factual recall but trails Claude Opus 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index.

- On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, a weighted average of nine tests of knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, mostly using private test sets, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks first (59, $7.76 and 21.6 minutes per task), ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. It costs less per task than Claude Opus 5.5, but more than GPT-6 Astra. - Carbon ranks first on four of the nine individual Intelligence Index tests: AutomationBench-AA, which measures performance on business tasks; HLE-Diamond, expert-level academic questions revised from Humanity’s Last Exam; Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, research tasks in the sciences carried out in a terminal; and AA-Omniscience v1.1, which measures general knowledge against hallucination rates. - On Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index v2.0, which tests combinations of models and harnesses on three coding benchmarks, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning running in Google’s Antigravity CLI ranks second (59, $7.74 and 29.8 minutes per task). It trails Claude Opus 5.5, but Carbon costs less per task and finishes faster. - On Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2, eight finance, coding, legal, and tax benchmarks weighted by each sector’s share of U.S. gross domestic product, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks second (70.45 percent accuracy, $10.51 and 47.75 minutes per task), trailing only Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning, while again costing less and finishing faster. - On Arena.ai’s Text Arena leaderboard, which ranks models via blind head-to-head comparisons, Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first (1,528 Elo), ahead of Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5. - Gemini 4 Carbon leads all models on three challenging cybersecurity benchmarks: CWE-bench (71.0%), ExploitGym (54.8%), and SEC-bench Pro (88.2%). These scores are self-reported.

Behind the news: Gemini 4 Carbon arrived around two weeks after Google made Gemini 4 Argon broadly available, and just a day after Artificial Analysis revised (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fd3prCCW8wLKSR6lZ3mKW6FZv2R3pZvSYW4jrMYV7S7QmlW2dK3BG5PxRqKW1lMH6N5RRgGDW8W5t1X3XVcTJVTqbhy8fVjXQM2c9LcwYz32MkgcNZ6dd4NW781BMV6pBp-ZW7KvWVQ3s_WGkW8DJdjJ128SgxW63v90J3YjL6CW4xc81F3fnNV3W4gPpFZ89pw6CW81f9Lk4V1jxkW90FlYm6w9xjWW47xs0D8MmK4CW2VY42299rfQSW4flWLG1PZ9rrN1Jwf-DkCjSvVWQM3N5K8mcLW3ZzHjx8nDl3pW6WJDhc5gNJGkW3Shx538MHt_6W398mVk4WN-55W2M9ghl3YKqNpW3ffdjH1j2df0W6p-fMN48Lwjhf5vrF-s04 ) its Intelligence Index. The updated Index swaps in more demanding tests and splits the score evenly among knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge. Models’ scores on version 5.0 don’t compare directly with those of earlier versions. For example, Kimi 3.1 Pro, the best-performing open weights model, was just three points behind Claude Opus 5.5 using the old Index; now it is 12 points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and 13 points behind Gemini 4 Carbon.

Why it matters: Once Gemini 4 Carbon’s introductory discount ends, it will cost exactly what Claude Opus 5.5 costs per token. Yet on Artificial Analysis’ Index, it finishes tasks with 29 percent fewer output tokens and costs 23 percent less per task. As frontier models converge on price and score, token efficiency becomes an increasingly competitive feature.

We’re thinking: Google CEO Sundar Pichai introduced Gemini 4 Carbon by reminding (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3lcW7L69QF1FDJ2dW3V0Rl53LD-SLW3t9y986jQG6HMvwwXtGrFXjW2CLxk-3QSg2sW1K5Fkk4lZ35wW7lZl49738S9hW8kwHbt7fRkBgW7Q2jnf5VbbkvW5qbN4f8pyY9jW2wnrBl1r7-zKW3Dzgbw4q19B0V3L-fn2GQqGzW1_kfP81jqmjvW8D_J-J9lPXm-W6qgzkK3YXxmsW1kv8GM2NVgvTW2KT0JM3P9w45W1CDByB10Lv1SVw40hS1Zn2jMW78BBn636MQkFN6gyrc78lVQFW3QvD-J64jspdTqf3X4cZn_0W5yQ_Kv6Qyct3W56njc_6RpFQHf1Gd8KR04 ) followers that he’d said Google would release models “periodically.” Two frontier models within a few weeks is an impressive pace. Gemini 4 Carbon’s 9-point lead over Gemini 4 Argon on Artificial Analysis’ index shows that frequent releases can bring big gains. We hope Google maintains this rapid rhythm.

Anthropic Pursues A Public Offering

Claude’s maker will sell company shares to the public for the first time. Anthropic’s financial statements show first-half revenue that grew 14-fold from a year earlier, an operating profit in the second quarter, and $895 billion in commitments to buy computing power.

What’s new: On October 26, Anthropic filed an S-1 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fx3prCCW95jsWP6lZ3kCW7T5MSV25bqvYVFtMWs8M6hynW2v8wTH5N3l-DW6TlWlJ2V8TfVW8_CgXY1dlvrhW1DyMbS40xBmnW98Hh_z4YZ_q3W6ZK4nr6kjwggW4cH8P63QnDWsW5nYN-V4_-hj-W7H1dJl2kw69wMx9fjnrBHfYVWZ2bj2LK42jW5dt3Dq7Y0N03W1LDHk83rXGpBW6MR0L591Hj8NW6kf4wZ6-yHg2W2t0-nd3H7jgJN5-FSFT3hqZrW52-d491qmSR2W54HRJm6JBKwfW4rx19s1BjjXQW5v3VQV5N0bGFW7rs-8x3tr7XpW38dqHR38nMRWW3X2JHm4ll--kW3Dmlvr99-rHZW1Zl5B27JxT-NW1z4L4f5FHJQnN6CSyvlzb3yrf60FSPC04 ) , the registration statement a company must submit to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission before it goes public. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker ANT. According to the filing, the offering’s main purposes are to increase Anthropic’s capital and financial flexibility and to create a public market for its shares. Anthropic plans to use the money to support its continued growth, including much-needed compute and infrastructure.

The offering: Anthropic could go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving and hopes to sell roughly $100 billion (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fd3prCCW8wLKSR6lZ3pXN2WMm9tJK4JyW5h_n7X275wHHW5M6lcF1mbjr1W4njp4Q2VkgpSW67kZW27-dYdYW94kBH876KPsSW7V3BV68rw5FZW5ncGKC8rpXgJW8jDmHj5Thl-gW7G29Dl4fYm1tW5m15hK7bLvx_W3DrmxS82sNh1W1G2B138Zx_pwVpCqP373Jc9bW6cHZHv73x1Q3V1yclw22YRGSW4qzHCl8TlG3BW1N5WDG7r4Jq7W5LBRBK8LTCD0N8gM429s2dWgW77Jdbk86y3_MW5gCwSW2C10NjW6r1LKx79tPq7W46tpQR6kMqljW2XK-F17SsC0KW8x64P460f675W8273pG79lnF9W6rjgFS8QL0nrf921bjC04 ) in shares, according to The Wall Street Journal. The filing leaves the final share price and total share count blank. Some investors expect Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cs5m_5PW50kH_H6lZ3nSW3_2CTH7nQpvFW2Gzq7b1kr7LzW549WNb4GcftwW2H8WQ73VKd22W3dCT1q5QGj9mW3fqC_X1_7tpkMbGxqMG-5_XW8QYd0c4XB7VQW2K1hsl49q7xJW5wsyqJ57L1phW3ySCRB7Wyfm2W7FwmKD47lT76W1gh5J_4CXJqsW5mvh8d3yWqntW14XjWL8LdSmSW80zXQL5TqVkRW4tz8Kj5JGBtLW2yX5RX9l7-HHW1wBnVg7WlsWzW5QMYL26YzpyZW1jJtWs2WPRgyN7qG6S8L8RSDW4Wj41X8GTY03W88LbvT26-ZjJW6YK8NZ1cRB7jW7dLvsn7gKvdcW3fcJKG69_DzmW9clCn12zbW9rW8s5_xf55KTWPW8yM8bb6ccJx5W3Gp2755x-LDLVpHW9Z8053kPf2Ktwxn04 ) , according to Bloomberg.

Who’s in charge: Public shareholders will get almost no say in the company’s future direction. A single share held by a company owned by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, carries 50.1 percent of the vote on most matters, and its voting power will automatically remain at 50.1 percent if Anthropic issues more stock.

The numbers: Anthropic’s revenue is growing much faster than its spending, even accounting for the growing cost of compute.

- Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Anthropic says it doesn’t expect revenue to keep growing quite that fast. In 2026’s second quarter, Anthropic earned an operating profit (revenue minus the costs of running the business) of $974 million on $11.6 billion in revenue, its first in any period the filing reports. - The company’s quarterly compute and infrastructure expenses rose from $944 million in early 2025 to $5.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026, but compute and infrastructure’s share of revenue fell from 251 percent to 48 percent. - Under standard accounting rules, Anthropic lost $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, but most of that came from an accounting adjustment, not money the company spent. Day-to-day operations brought in $3.9 billion in cash. - Anthropic has committed to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on computing power, often with companies that also finance it. Named deals include about $161.2 billion in rent on equipment from the chipmaker Broadcom, at least $114.5 billion with Google, at least $110 billion with Amazon, and up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI, under agreements that either party can cancel after early 2027. Google and Amazon both invested early in Anthropic, a relationship that the S-1 warns could lead to conflicts of interest. - The S-1 reveals that Anthropic’s Claude wrote more than 90 percent of the contributions to Anthropic’s codebase in September 2026. However, the filing says that using AI to build more capable AI in this way “could also pose a considerable safety risk.”

Risk disclosures: The S-1 laid out both conventional and unusual risks for a mainstream American technology company.

- Government sanctions could pose a future risk. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, two configurations of what was then Anthropic’s most capable model. To comply, Anthropic switched off both models for every customer, while its other models stayed available. It restored them once Commerce lifted the restrictions. - Disagreements with the Pentagon could cost Anthropic business, including with other government agencies and to companies that sell to the U.S. government. In February, after Anthropic said its technology shouldn’t be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President directed federal agencies to stop using it. The Department of Defense then designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cM5m_5PW5BWr2F6lZ3lsW4dXpNn8453_rW1hxXQ02-DKtsW2ktL2l3w210VW78PwY852sP0CVJSr5Z1KDvYYW4lxLS24RXT7ZVrMHWr1qDsg8N5Xp_7_yN_b_W16j3ZK4rkJsPN128c2B1nD1FW2z7TGZ5nkHhSVzwzf683Ng8kVG-hcc2ghcPGN40LH-tpH9NGW36VL2z500rKzW5Tzcm12pFd72W2rnZK73c_6VCW39jkr123zghWW6Yw1yG4S1fThW6RPhfF2yBvWGW8wNNxT6WYGK-W314tp84j-CR0W2fWFlP6k0kbgN4x45zwn0VKjW2StnYp1x-_S_W1yRqqZ8gHBxsW5cKyV75dRDPRW3LWxBG8XCSyGVQ5zMQ47Cl0xN1z9qyb2WLFZW1tJH_P3GdjyNW5d2jdG9hTjw3W2s0KJn6d_PTXW8thSl27q-6hQf8PmZN604 ) under two different laws. The final result of the dispute is still pending in court. - Like other labs, security lapses during model testing expose the company to potential liabilities. During pre-release cybersecurity tests built by an outside partner, a setup error left models connected to the Internet. Four Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to real third-party computer systems. Anthropic found no evidence that any model pursued goals beyond its assigned task. It suspended some of those tests. - The filing also notes concerns, raised inside Anthropic as well as by outside researchers and regulators, that sufficiently advanced AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without appropriate safeguards.

Why it matters: For developers using Claude, the filing should be more reassuring than alarming. Anthropic held $112.4 billion in cash at the end of June and turned an operating profit in the second quarter, which testifies to the company’s stability. Even export restrictions (the most direct hit to customers so far) proved temporary. Anthropic restored the models once the U.S. government lifted them and released updated versions in September.

We’re thinking: Within just a few years, Anthropic has gone from a promising startup to potentially a trillion-dollar company — kudos to the whole Anthropic team for this tremendous work! Stock valuations aside, Anthropic’s robust financials should help legitimate an industry that some critics have argued is overhyped. We’re less sure what to think about the filing’s risk factors: They’re a mix of sci-fi scenarios and genuine risks with implications that are difficult to forecast. We’re hopeful that public investment will help Anthropic continue to improve its products for years to come — and let their present performance, rather than speculative future scenarios, speak for them.

World Models Become Robot Playgrounds

Google says that Genie 4, its latest world model, will be used in tandem with Gemini models to create digital practice spaces for robots, giving them endless worlds to train in. So far, though, Google’s demos suggest there’s still a long way to go.

What’s new: On October 27, Google announced Genie 4 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fd3prCCW8wLKSR6lZ3l0W1S--Zf3MYY7GW6SC5bj1SrcmQW5fK5tk6PBXntW2-4Gc96CfM0HN7P80hzmdDfSW6rdL_C8nJPltW5fN9yt3TfY0bW2wK1MF5DfJFjW20s61p160q6lW4xfx-v6B_z1dN2hz4k_rW3ZRW4S_mrd3HPSq7W7bLCq-2S2ZW9W5Nr7HQ7BzpqLW978qMx4nffdxV2cngs6RfqlBN4WjJJGQ8wk1W4zQ11c7CvjsrW94b2St15t4cBN668BsqVz05SW4zNPpl3jh6S4W30kMD23lVJRtN8jnZrz2G-T5W3hLc_p2YJz4ZVX7ZBV5lNnZCW4y44BN9fLNVqW5sxHsk3DrNbZN2dP9LjkYzh3f34JyCn04 ) , which it has released to a limited group of testers in a research preview. Genie 4 produces interactive worlds that Google says are even more realistic than its predecessor, Genie 3. Users can change a scene midway through with a text prompt, but now Gemini models help work those changes into the scene. Genie 4 also adds sound, which allows it to create real-time audio for each world it generates, whether it’s two people chatting on a motorcycle or snow crunching under a crowned crane’s feet. Google AI Ultra subscribers as well as some developers should be getting access in the weeks ahead.

How it works: Genie 4 doesn’t have a technical report out yet, but Google’s announcement explains how Gemini models can help direct what Genie 4 renders.

- Navigation: Users move through a scene with video game-style mouse and keyboard controls. - Text directions: While Genie 4 renders a scene, Gemini 3.8 Flash (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dF3prCCW7lCdLW6lZ3lvVMVKBF1JgJk5W3rQ-vk4vFW5FW2fchfM1MTWkYW9k02MG3n6llXN9g2Qk462MfsW4g5KR59fZbtxW7vwnYr9jrD1TW9gvbxP2vQ-K_N3Cr7WgsmS-0W6Bys5t7LYc24W3-wn0x75CWt4Vs9Vzc3XGk9HW5wgZXS55756RW8Mrqmv8NKpcXW2GQjQg1yhlJ2VVZF3N4XSxhCW4S7hGZ7rM9vSW14Bw1v9m0RYGW3HDDDF484WqlV5WBwx1GssHPW3sVrDF4T1BsmW3xM2x58C9PZrMGD2R-L3D_7N1qwPZH2Z7JGf8s3n6H04 ) works alongside it as a director. It breaks the user’s goal into steps, then double-checks each new frame to make sure each of those steps has been executed, adjusting its plan if the user inserts changes as things go along. - Video: Gemini Omni (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fd3prCCW8wLKSR6lZ3kXW4b5_pL3S_PkhVzD1243kt-rrW12B9LX715gXrW5_rRVK8LbJGQN6qrNx5LD6wsW6_3jbN36JV5-W3PkWyN7qfJPVW433cvC6GyyDmW1YCTZj6F8TyzW87P_gg2pxsl9W55nr9P7q6vpCW3Wvjzk3P68TGVvxVXh8Qr28_W75fvXJ4H0Y-DW30VJNr4LX97RW4rdLbT55_kTVVQJLbY5j5J1kW9k56LL7p4c4pN3YQj_-hnZsCW4v26f34QXyqWW3mF05d7FF938N2b-rSx5lQ9TW7pyCDR7Lr3pKW5Xj1VM27tz8_W4TD0nw2S71kvW41sf6H1q485XN50t3dJ54Mz4W5l_CHx1zKhqMf928f7Y04 ) , Google’s video generation model, helps Genie 4 render more realistic scenery. Google demoed examples including a maple seed gracefully spinning and landing on grass, as well as people shuffling along a 1980s-era train platform. - Robotics: In a demo, Google’s reasoning model Gemini 4 Argon (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9fx3prCCW95jsWP6lZ3n1W4tckpl8HGZhfW3bbF346ZSPNWW4x5FTg117NRJW2dQGcw1BLgsnW5tTbJq2Yj2rJW85y6cp28pkW3W4cWkTP6TWGd8VcqPVv1LXc0pW8c6Sb07RBC6kW1j2XNn7kzwZXW4gDNb-2L9pc8W1q_VWN6sktrkW161_yY31V-71W42ljc63XwXgYW1Kh2dK4XqDm_W3gDWZ-8KfkrkW129pQq5QgN2WW6fbXMX49S2sYW876YK562K4y9N4Wg1sL7dghgW4t0Z6D2VF2ykW4tGjqp73R-pTW8mvNgp2T5B-qW7-JBlt23Gdk-W5Nt_y81ZSmqRW6kbsVM1nDKk4W6pM4wc6tmfNdW1Q1hp57N2XYNVjP-CK6TjZ4lW6vzP4-4S3t0Kf3g2jY404 ) broke a task into text-based steps for Genie 4 while it rendered a simulation of Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers with a person. Google didn’t describe a robot control system in the loop.

Results: Google’s announcement was full of curated demos, but the company didn’t offer any quantitative evaluations to back them up. Google says a simulation can run up to two minutes, roughly double Genie 3’s limit, but DeepMind research engineer Hang Qi noted that reaching that limit doesn’t guarantee that a scene will keep its consistency the whole time, according to Bloomberg (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cs5m_5PW50kH_H6lZ3nPW6D_jYh6H5dyvW2VFmSh3Mr9SDW4pCnkg7-_BxKW4YmfCx1MpYTJW5jmVQ46hmw_SW1bP_JK4JfVp8W8YLbC84Xp_7zW363dwd3qBPVqW9hcnzD8J8RGzV4xZph3jXPJcN5Zhy37KxzpbW3dgkzl7ppxxbW3Vv02b6GbGPZW2g52-21Z9xh6N1cf_zc8V9pmW13Kws02c_SdKW1X3XSp93p1sbW4KN-WZ7BzCGmW8vMQT24LsmH4W8br-pN72YxnkW4SVYMG1CY4bYW3RRfZN93xC5HW1jwGt34rzLcqN8CZ2SRnxnTSN7tNjgytVXc2W99nB6j6VBX9jW5hRyqJ5P21_CW703CqT73JS-ZW1vkz6n3wxfnqW58-mTp5HNC3ZW6QZqYm4pbrjsN7nptMLv2-lQdVFNTM04 ) . Google says it’s still working to improve complex physical interactions. One of its demos even includes a physics slip: A marble bust that drops onto a watermelon settles on its plinth when it should topple over the side. “There’s only so much that you can do with two minutes,” Google DeepMind product manager Diego Rivas said, according to TechCrunch (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cM5m_5PW5BWr2F6lZ3msW3NpQ-b41lz9LN8m-kN_BbgFMW5QGgPx6RN8YvW6pNpsV3cHsJWW1hp9GF7T9KCqW1-7r-M7dxJkKW63vXvx4X_pQ1W3JXNhN8hJ3XvVJFzyK5yjh8YW8x30rY1fDQYKW65VPky72hgLHVH8MRG1MPFlgW6JH0rH7GTlYZW428jN48gQkLbW37B8Gk7Z49P3N5ZJ_PBLm6GrW5X3qt098nRf_W31D7_m2_gTsKVKFffD7Y5_PfMsqybksPHDqW66VwVQ6j59VZW1Lw-kn6Z6NZzW1C4lXM7q6xLxW2dQt3r5SpwYsW7HnGKn54R_9cF3zy53ZgrfmW7l_VGY63B7VVW2kGW5N8_8bFZN4134N_sv7mBW19QxB54WXVrFN6SHKyY6SPJTW7zg9kv92cTfdW8j1c8Z2ZZtSWW5Bgpk32btDpLdYlwdx04 ) . “We’re still in the research journey. We’re not necessarily in the end product journey.”

Behind the news: Genie 4 has plenty of company. The world models field is getting more crowded, although not every world model operates the same way. Like GWM Worlds 2 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dF3prCCW7lCdLW6lZ3nrW4_WH5N6nCvkjW5-dQ6S5wpJcGW5K95Dx4pyB_pW1tTkfN13v0c5W2GqZrB3P3ND4W89_bWB2pDTZpW1f_YQ35w831JN3bgyXvPzYNTN3Qt2kLgV_45W4LZkNT1NtX21W7sK9jY5XhjczW9kPyVl2-fyYxW55FX2r8YcSNtW5WdWFs4ktn6NN56Wv64KyXmsW7QM7M01fS7dzW1r464h8rCzhGW7h2m854CVQfCVYD5Qj4MH10KW5hsQts5jk7L_N5Z6_S8d4kF0W6KY3n82h1LkYW3tlzqw6kpH5HW5rxfc72Lmr8Wf83D_9z04 ) , the model Runway released in September, Genie 4 generates video in real time. Marble (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dl3prCCW6N1vHY6lZ3kWW2-RQLf8X7GYHVfgFqK56DYBKW1Hpz9X14CfGPW2S672K64vcv9W8Fk4-z2FWXN2W67rK265pwgPGW3V-hQR4PfRtcW4jqCp26V1gSnW2gSkcf7dDl8ZW1_1Sqw5hxDJnW5dpGm-6vWW-nW1HwmwJ3hrws8W92j68M3jhWGRW235L7_3yw5hgW6QjFr636Nf70W4-sWvX1kQ2QNVx8scl6q8zJ_V7vX2k2LhdB7W18w3W67LPQJ6W6_DR-b1hppj7VHdNL14pbYY_W1h61t123PdMmf3xz8bn04 ) , from AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s startup World Labs, and HY-World 2.0 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dF3prCCW7lCdLW6lZ3nFW4J-Kpc6Mw7KZW4yPc4G41x1D9W8N_n2D23fQjgVFKpF23K60pLW5XpCQ36V-jDwW4r5nbc5x8C1vW8mHrNH3YcGVMW2dZMQF7gg2GnVWCzPb4ZZm_mTy7h55HNQZxW13TFJz1xYFPfW22QKFH91wszPVBb8J626tDJWVncM878sgwYyW9kJ0hF1RbgB5W4y8qZV3nl3qdVmr-0R61HzYwW7d3jMw1gKKWvW7s6Cyg1NjKNZVwvW1q7CyfPyN1X9QD0-GP97W8GG4Gz54G1-cN87rkqxWQ1jvW2hNy9n6S-4Wdf7mz5LY04 ) , an open-weights model from Chinese tech giant Tencent, build persistent 3D scenes instead. Like AI video companies, more and more world model companies have become robotics companies, or at least are pursuing applications of their models to robotics.

- Robotics isn’t the only field disrupted by the new wave of world models. When Genie 3 opened to paying subscribers in January, it sparked a sharp selloff of video game stocks. In October, electric-vehicle maker Rivian bought (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dl5m_5PW6N1X8z6lZ3nSW3sxNDY1C2tRMW8NsVbq8wmzLcW6Y6Tjw3TGfnrW4pRq566-MpkkN7fx4ntPXZKFW5SP0fD58ybnJW7DRNsr3Mqm-vW3m0BGx3L55_kW1wvSPv24LySwW5Xv2sY4GmwNBN46QWk8Jv-MdW2kKf2j4lZC-KW2_t__c4Zr6CtW7LLp513qCSXmW4DKrD-92jD9sW5KJ_qY2wJyn7W3z4xpD82bLsRN485D1lhYF72W34gJSQ6mT9rGW2-r3Qw4Ly1b6W6VdPrp1jmHkJW41KW6X741Lc9W8bbRX21bgrBkW1GGV2d3PL-jVW4Y2ZDD3BwpnyN72W0M9QM01bW5kKF6s5FN7JnW4zp69c1l_GLhW3MP50y4Nq-W-W6kNF_V46FwhPW9lGLLy1L4KJ-N7q-G-kRVSW2W39fssR7CGr8NW8S8_B_2c29J6W3dPR7v6L0299W69fJSD58WKq5W4JNJKV3tHcY5VG2GXn4pFMSkf5yj3dx04 ) world-model startup Third Dimension to bring self-driving simulation in house. - The field is also consolidating. AMD agreed in September to buy World Labs (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3m8W47_CyZ6btZ-6W6q2NQc62YCnJW5Zfr8S57McNpW6cClLj31fx-BW9k1lK08zswrJN1tY42ZKk6cTW6wnt833Xyff3V6DH9-96TSQJW3YCSYC2PV382W29Ccbh4hl5Y-W2-B9ds272hgZN7gydy7ty9qhVkkrdW2XZJsPW8N2rgt23wMcxW30hKBb4HHtykW3hrh9c91GX3FN4hcpL57x0hJN5qPQcnB93LdW2-cgW18RYjVkW4xbv3D4f5Dn9VqQNfm5SbhWZW1RgDjF6L5VngW8fmwjg73d4yKW4Y9yRs7fZWyDW5lcLRz3rlYTLW97ThXJ52c9SFf61ZtQl04 ) for about $8.2 billion, and Amazon has been in talks to acquire Decart, whose products include world models for robotics and driving simulation, according to The Wall Street Journal. (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cs5m_5PW50kH_H6lZ3l_N8JF2jp-XCMjW3ZlTbh1QmhgWW5Rr6Zt6k55FKW6PRcWF8xYM__W6Wg4825zCvzhW7Ysd0M70wtH4W3WtgK79l0QwhN4fsfKWpPwkpW4Rd3Rf3GmNPSW14QsN38X4Z_YW7NQNBy6R85b2W9454Hc2jWNDHW1dcNSH6g7hF2W16xSBh3d95NYW3CrX9g8y2z74W41rcmT4wMx31W2nSbsd40Km9KW68sSwX97DvsGW612ZYS6QxpcQW51qM_l8v2rFrW7gVNrn86Gm72N34ZcpJ6kN7MW75kc-12DbbGSW4835Fr5Z61vzW5rJB8g3ZHZDJVY-TmC5QVKB2VQDLK58nKbPsW3nD5sq58bbjQVk2zYF3cj5YxW98d4kc58ZbBBW5TMD7697trhXW59242C45q9Msf7L_0JP04 ) - Genie 3 served as an environment for SIMA, DeepMind’s agent for 3D virtual worlds. Waymo later built a driving simulator (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9cs5m_5PW50kH_H6lZ3m7N4jyBDP-dY29Mg4Y-77vv34W1K2Hxq3_cMn5W88GWcv8bDdnRW3zKLDK3zQbMLW40K6D387kQxgN7GdjsmgkjwDW2Dy68z3hMsrGN61bm2qBSN90VVghSD1rMC1KW5G-gBm5rzTC2W879R5S7s06tGW6nm_WH5rDtzvW2-Hl3f1PPWJ1W3MVb-D3p8jl-W7ZYHbx1tdHHKW46y0y28HQQ-xVCFhxp6CtFgBW2lHq2g94xvDWW23y1CZ2cpmKGW93Gkwf8991nDW6Hwzrv8Z77jdW2zNKhJ3Nz-L8W1DctSV26h5XmW9drR7z8CgFnZVKzPRg5cJhLmW1b6l2M7rGBT8W1Tm2nF2MLMr3V78JlX8nkvc0W5d0bMY41XGCqW3HwztS1-lZc0W5XWmfn1TMj_Kf5m0khF04 ) on Genie 3 to generate unusual scenarios (things like a tornado or an elephant in the road). - Runway has also pushed its world models toward robotics. In February, it announced (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3lLW5Xzrhx5w69s5W7Kkjxb3_Ty1hVJDnYS70DcVXVCS7vQ28WxpQW4-DJHR5FydQPN3c59f8GYdq3W8PSWxn7RTJV6W32TbQN97LMLCW47YNX32MvzGhW849rmd93xM3JN91v2q19KMLTW5kCpGf1cbmxKW3XmtcR5C3lBvW3NQpHR52vhp8W93V_KH21MPb9W8Wv7Hw7DKx-VN5zNywQtdDByW3xps8k1QKt-jW4cW8Md1CFrV_W46WWj-8pnpHXW2lGr7H13JHdkW5MZFD71DcjBvN3zM3MKRBHNNW7NWW121K8rxJVKg_CY6fr4P_W2_M0HM4rD91Pf2kw7rl04 ) that robot-control policies acting inside a robotics version of its video model earned simulated scores that closely tracked their real-world results in tabletop tests. In September, Runway debuted a research preview of GWM Worlds 2 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dF3prCCW7lCdLW6lZ3nrW4_WH5N6nCvkjW5-dQ6S5wpJcGW5K95Dx4pyB_pW1tTkfN13v0c5W2GqZrB3P3ND4W89_bWB2pDTZpW1f_YQ35w831JN3bgyXvPzYNTN3Qt2kLgV_45W4LZkNT1NtX21W7sK9jY5XhjczW9kPyVl2-fyYxW55FX2r8YcSNtW5WdWFs4ktn6NN56Wv64KyXmsW7QM7M01fS7dzW1r464h8rCzhGW7h2m854CVQfCVYD5Qj4MH10KW5hsQts5jk7L_N5Z6_S8d4kF0W6KY3n82h1LkYW3tlzqw6kpH5HW5rxfc72Lmr8Wf83D_9z04 ) , a real-time world model with audio. It also announced Praxis-1 (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dF3prCCW7lCdLW6lZ3kYW4g80by9htDJ8VcVnXX6W0n1cW8_70kK77pM0_W21T3JX8w3yTXW1lnp_X2mf4SvV3qT7C6jSL4gW6Qx3dQ7J03kPW2zy90K2KTg1hW4LgmVb6_pWqTVBHBdn23nrbVN64bRc_yNpLrW2M7M0k7-_x1rW6D_VC187q0rFN94xfvkMk2-yMgqnpcTLrG8W5B1Qjl6-v4LDW3wkJMb3jYX6JW7BK2DN4JS85pN2FFzLq6GrrfW2Tx2wW2j28s8W6pXLlY4pgLd_W4Mb08p4Cw_FtW2Jgf8z6238cxW12ZmC85DPLjBf6Cb_Qb04 ) , a model for controlling real robots that it plans to release with open weights.

Why it matters: Google’s clearest evidence that simulation can improve real robots comes from a different approach from other companies. A few weeks before Genie 4’s debut, Google showed (https://info.deeplearning.ai/e3t/Ctc/LX+113/cJhC404/VVZXDL4DVT_FW8B5MNt5GnpQVV_gMC15X0ysmN4xH9dY3prCCW7Y8-PT6lZ3k-W74cQkV6PZ3wQW5nHgWb444BR_W680VxF404drYN1q3sgCM4jWGW68SzBt1WTW6xW6t7K5w3GSqLxW6v3S5k2GKh7sW8N-rhl1Kb8QsW4zd87q6twhWCW5CTh401LmRyXM1ZfLGyQlCdW5235NB7BYf7mW2B1Nwb69zdk2W7QVBWN2yWR8sV63T2X3kgxqnVB0cL-81mrLxW2qr9YM5_tZxVW4-6Dmn5xW_LJW6jYfXf10bqBjVfQ5dY6qfQDJW3tYBCb3xq5n1W6HlWBw1LLCGQW5HPRL-6Ljp39W4Xgt6C7rNHVKW5WBNSC88mrB5W5dlJM_4JbPbmf4C-XMd04 ) Gemini 4 Argon writing physics simulations in the MuJoCo engine based on photos and video. From a single photo of a tabletop, Argon generated more than 4,500 practice episodes, and fine-tuning a robot-control model on them raised its real-world success rate from 56 percent to 75 percent. Google’s proposed path forward, which it calls hybrid world models, would combine elements of both the structured reasoning of language and code models with a generative model that renders pixels. Theoretically that could give generated environments reliable cause and effect, which is something video models often lack.

We’re thinking: A good robot simulator lets plans fail, since robots learn from mistakes as well as successes. Genie 4 pairs its renderer up with a Gemini director that checks whether each step of a plan succeeded. This can accidentally drift the world toward whatever the intended outcome is. In the marble bust clip, the model itself seems to choose a neat landing on the plinth instead of the toppling over the side like physics says it should. Our question for DeepMind: Can a plan fail in Genie 4? We’d like to see that Apptronik robot hand mess up and drop a few checkers, too.

Context Engineering for Images

Managing an agent’s context by storing all the input text it receives and giving it tools to search the text boosts its performance. For vision-language agents, the same is true of storing images.

Today’s top items:

1. Li Xi on the Plenum Resolution - As expected, Li Xi, Standing Committee member, CCDI head and deputy head of the Fifth Plenum Resolution drafting group has an article in the Thursday edition of People’s Daily, following articles Tuesday and Wednesday by Wang Huning and Cai Qi, the other two deputy drafting heads. Li’s article, translated here, is titled “Resolutely Following the Anti-Corruption Path with Chinese Characteristics 坚定走好中国特色反腐败之路”. He reminds everyone that the Party has had a lot of corrupt elements:

(2) Uphold no forbidden zones, full coverage, and zero tolerance, and resolutely remove every corrupt element. With the courage of “scraping poison from the bone” and “a warrior cutting off his own wrist”, the Party resolutely investigated and punished corrupt elements including Zhou Yongkang, Bo Xilai, Guo Boxiong, Xu Caihou, Sun Zhengcai, Ma Xingrui, Zhang Youxia, He Weidong, and Ling Jihua. It seriously investigated such problems as collusion between political and business interests; resolutely addressed corruption in fields where power, funds, and resources are concentrated, including finance, state-owned enterprises, energy, pharmaceuticals, and infrastructure construction; insisted on investigating bribe-taking and bribe-giving together; deeply punished new and concealed forms of corruption; and continuously carried out Operation Sky Net, never allowing corrupt elements to remain beyond the reach of justice. From the 18th CPC National Congress through September 2026, discipline-inspection and supervision organs nationwide opened 8.105 million cases and disciplined 7.922 million people, including 963 centrally managed officials. This fully demonstrates our Party’s tenacious will and steadfast resolve to oppose every instance of corruption, punish every corrupt official, and eliminate wrongdoing to the end.

（二）坚持无禁区、全覆盖、零容忍，坚决清除一切腐败分子。以刮骨疗毒、壮士断腕的勇气，坚决查处周永康、薄熙来、郭伯雄、徐才厚、孙政才、马兴瑞、张又侠、何卫东、令计划等腐败分子，严肃查处政商勾连等问题，坚决整治金融、国企、能源、医药和基建工程等权力集中、资金密集、资源富集领域的腐败，坚持受贿行贿一起查，深入惩治新型腐败和隐性腐败，持续开展“天网行动”，决不让腐败分子逍遥法外。党的十八大以来，截至2026年9月，全国纪检监察机关共立案810.5万件，处分792.2万人，其中处分中管干部963人，充分彰显了我们党有腐必反、有贪必肃、除恶务尽的顽强意志和坚韧定力。

2. China Media Group studies spirit of the Plenum - The China Media Group Party Leadership Group met to study the Plenum Resolution. The official readout gives a view into external propaganda priorities:

The meeting called for actively carrying out external promotion of the plenum’s spirit and telling the Communist Party of China’s story well. CMG must fully leverage its advantages in overseas communication, innovate its discourse system and forms of expression, fully present to the international community the great achievements and valuable experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era, and introduce the strategic tasks and major measures involved in ‘Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.’ It must carefully plan topics, proactively set the agenda, actively guide discussion, and excel at using comparisons across ancient and modern times and between China and the West to profoundly reveal the characteristics and strengths of China’s path of combating corruption. It must improve its overseas distribution capacity and its ability to conduct on-the-spot “disinfection,” produce a group of external propaganda products grounded in facts, viewpoints and data, and counter attacks and smears by the United States and the West. It must deepen “media diplomacy,” organize a series of media activities in light of the concerns of audiences in target countries, further present the positive image of the Communist Party of China, and effectively strengthen the international community’s understanding and recognition of the Party.

会议要求，要积极主动开展全会精神对外宣介，讲好中国共产党的故事。要充分发挥总台海外传播优势，创新话语体系和表达方式，向国际社会充分展现新时代全面从严治党的伟大成就和宝贵经验，介绍持之以恒推进全面从严治党的战略任务和重大举措。要精心策划选题，主动设置议题，积极引导话题，善于在古今中西的对比中，深刻揭示中国特色反腐败之路的特点和优势。要提高海外投送能力、就地“消毒”能力，推出一批有事实、有观点、有数据的外宣产品，反制美西方攻击抹黑。要深化“媒体外交”，结合对象国受众关切，举办一系列媒体活动，进一步展示中国共产党良好形象，切实增强国际社会的认知认同。

What A Day: In the Pete of the Moment

The war comes home... to Pete Hegseth.

Matt Berg

Nov 5

READ IN APP

WAR AND PEACE (OUT)

Will Pete Hegseth take the fall for the GOP’s devastating midterm defeat? Donald Trump is reportedly quizzing aides about swapping out his war guy.

You know things are looking bad for you when multiple news outlets publish stories about your career with headlines that all use the phrase, “knives out.” That’s what Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth woke up to this morning, amid feverish speculation in Washington, D.C. that he might become the scapegoat for the GOP’s disastrous showing in the midterms.

As Republicans process their election night smackdown — which cost them control of both the House and the Senate — many GOP lawmakers and officials have settled on a culprit: the Iran war. Trumpworld is now searching for the guy who did this, so long as it turns out to be anyone but the guy actually responsible for starting the conflict: Trump himself.

Hegseth has emerged as an obvious fall guy. He has served as the Iran war’s chief salesman ever since reportedly pushing the president to strike in February. In the following months, the former Fox News personality bashed journalists who scrutinized the war’s ever-changing objectives, sparred with lawmakers who inquired how much the campaign was costing taxpayers, and blatantly lied that Iran’s military was “nearing complete destruction.” In April, Hegseth declared a “decisive military victory.” In November, peace remains elusive.

The president has reportedly polled advisers on whether Hegseth should keep his job. “Hegseth is definitely on thin ice,” a Trump adviser told Axios. “It doesn’t mean the president forces him out. But there are complications.” Another person told the New York Post: “When the word ‘war’ is in your title then you might be the person in the crosshairs.”

Hegseth’s future remains uncertain, even if Trump doesn’t fire him.

One reason Trump might not give Hegseth the boot: Senate Democrats likely wouldn’t confirm his preferred replacements — and they certainly wouldn’t usher in another washed up Fox News bozo. “I have every intention to keep him,” Trump told ABC News. The president could target other Iran war architects instead, like Gen. Dan Caine or Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper.

So Hegseth might not be fired. That doesn’t mean he’s in the clear. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) plans to introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, when the House returns. “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” Massie tweeted.

“They probably have the votes” to impeach Hegseth in the House, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) told a small group of reporters on election night. “I think there will be a lot of Republicans that’ll be just really pissed off [that they] fell for this bullshit from this president and Pete Hegseth.”

Trump knows that the war hurt the GOP’s election odds. “If we never went into Iran, what do you think would happen in the midterms?” he once privately asked someone. The question is what he does next.

WHAT ELSE? 👀

Harmeet Dhillon, a top Department of Justice official, resigned from her post today. She earned a reputation as one of the Trump administration’s most aggressive attack dogs, spending much of her time battling so-called “woke ideology” while leading the DOJ’s civil rights division.

First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian diplomats at the White House today, praising them for coordinating a temporary ceasefire in a small Russian-controlled Ukrainian town. Melania said she hopes the truce will lead to something “more enduring than a temporary ceasefire.”

The 2028 chatter has begun. Allies of Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) launched a group to support his likely campaign for president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio might resign and launch his own bid. And Vance basically laid out his presidential platform in a tweet yesterday. I expect this to be a huge topic at Crooked Con this weekend — get your tickets while you still can!

A top Iranian official mocked Vance, after the veep blamed Trump’s war in Iran for causing Republicans’ to lose the midterms. “Losing gambler energy, can’t walk away from the table,” tweeted Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaker of Iran’s parliament. “Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?”

A key panel is expected to approve Trump’s massive arch project today, a crucial step to begin construction. A federal judge could block or allow the construction as soon as today.

Justice Samuel Alito told his friends that he doesn’t plan to immediately retire, even as Republicans have a narrow window to replace him before Democrats officially take control of the Senate in January, the New York Times reports. Hold on a second: This guy has friends?

LIGHT AT THE END… ☀️

Gov Gavin Newsom (D-CA) spared the lives of all 548 inmates on death row in California, marking the largest commutation of prisoners facing death sentences in U.S. history. “State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us,” Newsom wrote in an open letter. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”

Tech broligarch Elon Musk was arguably the biggest loser of the midterm elections. He spent nearly half-a-billion dollars on races, and only three of the 37 Republican candidates he backed have won. Six of the seven Senate candidates he backed also lost — and it’s too close to call the final race involving Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK). Shares of Tesla and SpaceX also fell on Wednesday, as investors fear that Democrats will launch investigations into Musk and his businesses. Lol.

Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Jack White, Sia, Ne-Yo and other musicians were named as this year’s nominees for the 2027 Songwriter’s Hall of Fame. Members of Blondie, America, and ZZ Top also made the cut. A haw, haw, haw, haw, a haw.

The kids are into bluegrass music these days, apparently. “In the increasingly digital world, I think that young people appreciate the raw, acoustic and vintage feel of these older tunes,” Sam Wilson, the upright-bassist of Mountain Grass Unit (which is exclusively composed of twentysomethings) told the Washington Post. “It’s an escape from social media and the digital [world]. It’s something that’s real — and it’s as real as it gets.” You can catch me hootin’, hollerin’, and swingin’ on the dance floor.

Chihuahuas might be descendants of coyotes, which were domesticated “by the Toltec civilization around the turn of the first millennium,” according to a new study written up in the New York Times. This story has one of the best ledes I’ve ever read: “A casual observer might assume Chihuahuas are descended from angry electric toothbrushes.”

A web designer made a game where you can guess U.S. state fish. This is very fun, even though I got every single one wrong.

Back to War?

Weighing a post-election escalation with Iran. Also: the Global Briefing news quiz, the global youth revolt, and Trump’s great ‘repudiation’ by voters …

ADVERTISEMENT

Thursday, November 5, 2026 View in browser

Insights, analysis and must reads from CNN’s Fareed Zakaria and the Global Public Square team, compiled by Global Briefing editor Chris Good

Seeing this newsletter as a forward? Sign up here.

Back to War?

Now that the midterms are over, will the US and Iran return to more active hostilities?

As the US elections approached, President Donald Trump signaled he did not want to escalate the war before Americans voted. He also mused, in his UN General Assembly speech in September, about destroying Iran completely. And he also said the war would end soon after the elections.

All that has pointed toward a post-election resumption of airstrikes, perhaps followed by a peace agreement. Is that still the likely trajectory?

Many are bracing for it, Le Monde’s Claire Gatinois and Louis Imbert write. But the decision is Trump’s to make, which means unpredictability. The value of any US military operation against Iran “is no longer measured in terms of American strategic interests, but in terms of symbols,” Alex Vatanka of the DC-based, Gulf-backed Middle East Institute tells the Le Monde reporters. “It’s about making Donald Trump look strong.”

New strikes might make Trump look “strong,” but the war is unpopular. Vice President JD Vance blamed it for Republicans’ midterm losses, and Trump did not dispute that. Even if Trump is looking for a way out of the conflict, “the midterm results do not offer a guarantee of a quick resolution to the war,” Miranda Jeyaretnam writes for Time. Iran, seeing advantage in Trump’s newfound political weakness, might “harden its stance in negotiations” and demand concessions, making it more difficult for Trump to accept a war-ending settlement. “Trump has accepted the criticism of the cost” of the war, “but not the premise,” international-relations professor William Figueroa, of the Netherlands’ University of Groningen, tells Jeyaretnam. And Trump “has little else to lose should he decide to pursue another escalation,” Figueroa adds.

Then again, Trump might have little to gain beyond looking tough temporarily. In a Middle East Institute discussion on Wednesday, former US Ambassador Ryan Crocker was asked what another round of airstrikes could achieve, given that the larger, original salvo—dubbed Operation Epic Fury—did not force Iran to capitulate to US demands in spring. “I would say it would be absolutely zero percent chance” that a smaller aerial blitz would secure Trump’s war goals, Crocker said. “I think it would … simply intensify Iranian determination to hold out and, where possible, to escalate against the US. That would be the absolute worst thing we could do. And I would imagine that this is what the president is mulling over in his mind and probably discussing with Israeli Prime Minister [Benjamin] Netanyahu. … Kinetic action is not going to weaken or topple the [Iranian] regime in any way, shape or form. They’ve been through far worse with the Iran–Iraq War” of the 1980s.

Meanwhile, US allies will watch warily. At The Standard, Nicholas Cecil warns: “if Iran comes under new attack it is likely to lash out at America and its allies in the Middle East and Europe including the UK.”
