Musk’s Big Bet

According to the latest available figures, Elon Musk contributed at least how much money to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections?

a) $225 million

b) $445 million

c) $695 million

d) $815 million

To see the answer, read to the end of this newsletter.

Trump Train Stopped at Repudiation Station

“It was Donald Trump’s day, but not in a good way,” writes the right-leaning Colorado Springs Gazette editorial board, which endorsed the president in 2020. The “Trump effect” was “pronounced in race after race” as the president’s unpopularity dragged down Republican candidates across the board.

As others have also argued, conservative commentator Chris Caldwell writes in a New York Times op-ed that Democrats won big not because their party is suddenly popular but because of Trump’s missteps. From immigration enforcement to his attacks on university DEI initiatives to launching the Iran war, Trump overreached. Many voters might support enhanced border security and a more orderly immigration process, for instance, but ICE’s spectacle of cruelty and violence turned them off, Caldwell argues. Broadly, he asserts, “Mr. Trump’s vanity has destroyed his second term.”

In other words, Tuesday’s vote was a fulsome “repudiation,” as another conservative commentator, Yuval Levin, writes for the National Review, revisiting an analytical theme of his. “The American electorate has been repudiating the status quo again and again, but our political leaders have refused to offer something different,” Levin writes. Election results in 2016, 2020 and 2024 all were rejections of the status quo, in Levin’s view.

“In each case,” Levin writes, “the public rendered a negative verdict on the loser, not a positive verdict on the winner.” Although Levin depicts Trump as cartoonish, and his cult of personality as “a nihilistic, post-constitutional Caesarism utterly unworthy of a free people,” he also sees little positive affinity for Democrats among the American electorate. “We have been living through what you might call a politics without winners,” Levin argues. “As I wrote two years ago, in the immediate wake of Trump’s [2024] win … ‘This is the trap that our 21st-century presidents have tended to fall into. They win elections because their opponents were unpopular, and then—imagining the public has endorsed their party activists’ agenda—they use the power of their office to make themselves unpopular.’ This election should teach both parties that lesson again, but it will still be hard to learn.”

The Global Youth Revolt

Follow the link below to watch

Why are young people protesting all over Europe and beyond? On Sunday’s GPS, Fareed examined the sources of their anger.

News Quiz: The Answer Is …

Question: According to the latest available figures, Elon Musk contributed at least how much money to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections? Answer: $445 million

“The world’s richest man has contributed more than $445 million to federal committees alone through mid-October,” CNN’s Fredreka Schouten wrote—“more than double the nearly $177 million that Democratic megadonor George Soros gave to outside groups during the 2022 cycle to become the largest known individual donor in the last midterm elections for Congress.”

Reuters’ Dawn Kopecki, Sheila Dang, Alexandra Ulmer and Virginia Furness add: “Musk spent $445 million on federal races alone, according to nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets. The full extent of his money’s reach may never be known. He spent tens of millions more through dark money nonprofit groups—which disclose less about their donors than political action committees—a person familiar with his campaign spending said, and millions more on state and local elections that do not have uniform disclosure ​rules, local media outlets have reported.”

“Silicon Valley billionaires who courted Donald Trump and donated more than $600mn to Republican candidates suffered heavy losses in the US midterm elections, as voters anxious about the rise of AI and Big Tech,” the Financial Times’ Joe Miller, Michael Taffe and George Hammond write, hearing from one GOP operative who helped coordinate Big Tech political spending that, simply, “the money didn’t work.”

Voters broadly rejected Silicon Valley’s plans to build AI data centers around the country, as The Washington Post’s Miriam Waldvogel, Shira Ovide and Evan Halper detail. At The Atlantic, tech writer Charlie Warzel sees a broad backlash against large tech firms and their multi-billionaire owners—and suggests Musk typifies the kind of tech oligarch voters don’t want having too much power. In recent years, Silicon Valley has warmed to the MAGA movement, evincing “loud and proud anti-wokeness” in some cases, Warzel writes; Musk himself was empowered to gut the federal bureaucracy through DOGE.

“All of this seems to have rubbed many Americans the wrong way,” Warzel writes. “A majority of Americans in exit polls expressed deep concern about government corruption and also artificial intelligence. This election cycle, Musk appeared to represent almost every faction America has indicated that it is tired of right now. He is the oligarch class, data centers and AI, MAGA politics and cronyism all rolled into one man. Now Musk and the tech leaders will have to recalibrate their politics for a Congress that may be actively hostile to their interests.”

NEWSLETTER · 05 Nov 2026, 23:32

What’s troubling JD Vance

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next. By JACK BLANCHARD Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. This is Jack Blanchard, writing this new

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next.

By JACK BLANCHARD

Send tips here | View in your browser

Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. This is Jack Blanchard, writing this newsletter fresh off a flight to the U.K., where the U.S. midterm elections remain top of the headlines. Or at least they did until the Russell Brand trial verdict came in mid-afternoon. Drop me a line.

5 THINGS THAT MATTERED TODAY

— Counting continued in knife-edge U.S. Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska, with Democrats increasingly confident of landing both seats.

— The Nasdaq tanked as investors processed what Democratic control of Congress and key state governorships might mean for the AI industry.

— Flights in Europe were hit with a second wave of false bomb alerts.

— The Bank of England raised U.K. interest rates for the first time in three years, and warned of further hikes if the Iran War is not resolved.

— The Saudi- (and Trump)-backed LIV golf project was finally wound up.

THE NEXT NEWS CYCLE

U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally on Nov. 2, 2026 in Swanton, Ohio. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images

LIKE AS WAVES MAKE TOWARD THE PEBBLED SHORE: If Tuesday night was the beginning of the end of the Trump era — and it absolutely was — then it should be no surprise that minds in Washington have turned so quickly to what comes next.

Vice President JD Vance’s 600-word thought bubble on the underlying reasons for the Republican Party’s devastating midterm losses will be remembered as the moment the GOP’s 2028 primary race began.

Vance’s X post was a transparent attempt to start moving the conservative conversation beyond Tuesday’s crushing defeat, and to begin to chart his own path for a post-Trump Republican Party. That to do so he felt the need to quickly distance himself from Trump’s war on Iran tells us much about the contest ahead.

Trump is, of course, historically unpopular. Barring some exceptional set of events, that’s unlikely to change much during his final years in office. Politicians rarely get more popular the longer they stay in power, and Trump shows little sign of trying to curry favor with voters by rethinking unpopular policies. Republicans, meanwhile, have now seen the electoral consequences of that unpopularity writ large.

That means every GOP 2028 wannabe now has a strategic decision to make. How far, and how fast, do they distance themselves from Trump?

Vance’s tentative first steps away from the president show just how difficult a tightrope this will be to walk. We all know Vance hated the war from the start — but even in the aftermath of an electoral hammering, he still felt obliged to dress his message up as “data” and to insist that Trump himself had said much the same.

There are good strategic reasons for this approach, beyond avoiding a standup row with the boss. Trump may have lost large parts of the country, but there are few signs yet that he’s lost his MAGA base. As recently as this summer we were all lauding the president’s enduring grip on his party as he breezily ousted long-serving and proven Republican senators like John Cornyn and Bill Cassidy.

Those were unwise decisions from an electoral perspective — Cornyn’s hopeless MAGA successor, Ken Paxton, was soundly beaten in Texas, while Julia Letlow only narrowly clung on in deep-red Louisiana. But they served as powerful reminders of Trump’s enduring hold over the Republican grassroots. It’s easy to forget amid Tuesday’s bloodbath that Trump will likely remain the GOP kingmaker come 2028.

Vance therefore knows he needs to stay close enough to Trump to win a Republican primary — but far enough away to win a general election later the same year. That’s going to be quite a challenge.

“It’s possible for him to modestly differentiate himself,” a Vance ally who is close to the White House told my POLITICO colleagues. “But there’s no way he can totally separate. He’s still Trump’s vice president. This is still a Trump administration war. They’re still both unpopular. He’s not as unpopular as Trump but he’s unpopular.”

The problem is not unique to Vance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is clearly not as closely tied to Trump as his vice-president is, but he’s plenty close enough that he faces the same dilemma. Rubio has not been the most enthusiastic supporter of Trump’s war in Iran. But he remains the nation’s top diplomat and national security adviser. His hands are not exactly clean.

U.S. State Department officials today laughed off rumors that Rubio is on the verge of quitting his post to launch a 2028 bid. There’s no reason to believe he will do so. But the fact such rumors get any kind of traction is testament to the 2028 dilemma Rubio would face, should he decide to run.

It’s reasonable to wonder, given the sense of damaged goods around Trump this week, if a 2028 Republican contender might not emerge from beyond the president’s sphere. Sen. Ted Cruz — moonlighting these days as a podcaster with an enormous following — would be one obvious candidate. He has huge name recognition in conservative circles and maintains an arm’s-length distance from Trump.

But he has also long been an advocate of regime change in Iran. On the very issue he most needed to diverge from Trump, Cruz is arguably the closest of all. His efforts this week to disown the war may have come too late.

All of which leaves the door open to the possibility of a true outsider emerging, Trump-like, to shake this race up. (My POLITICO colleague Alex Burns wrote about this here back in June.) Not even a newsletter called “Forecast” is going to predict who that might be. But in an age of seemingly endless public rage at those in authority, it’s surely possible that the same forces that propelled Trump to the top of his party re-awaken to anoint his successor.

One thing is certain. This week’s election results mean the coming Republican contest — along with the parallel Democratic race — is going to grip American politics for the next two years. Not since 2008 have both parties’ presidential primaries felt this wide open, with no obvious winner on either side.

The rest of the world will be hanging on every development. Trump’s MAGA movement has been highly destructive to many of the principles the rest of the Western world holds dear — free trade; respect for global institutions; the defense of Europe’s post-Cold War order. What comes next will be every bit as consequential.

FUTURE INTELLIGENCE

SAME OLD STORY: Woe betide any Western politician facing the electorate in its current mood.

The same public rage over the cost of living that swept away dozens of Republican members of the U.S. Congress this week now threatens the prime minister of New Zealand, which holds a general election on Saturday.

Kiwi PM Chris Luxom, a former airline executive, is battling to avoid becoming New Zealand’s first ever leader to be thrown out of office after just one term. Luzon leads a three-party conservative coalition currently running neck and neck with Labor opponents.

“His approval ratings are very poor,” Kiwi journalist Guyon Espiner told this week’s POLITICO Canberra Playbook Podcast. “There have been at least two attempts from his own party to actually get rid of him.” But both coup attempts failed, Guyon added, as Luxom’s National Party “didn’t have an alternative leader in the wings.”

The unpopularity of the nation’s leader will not be the only aspect of this election that sounds familiar to overseas readers.

“New Zealanders are extremely concerned about the cost of living,” Espiner said. “We had high inflation following COVID, and they have struggled to some degree to get on top of that. And we’ve had prices, especially for food and other basics like electricity and fuel, exacerbated by geopolitical issues — war and tariffs from the Trump administration. Cost of living is right at the top.”

The voting looks so tight that one of New Zealand’s smaller startup parties may well end up playing kingmaker in a post-election coalition. We’ll find out on Saturday whether Luxom has what it takes to buck the insurgent fever sweeping through voters around the world.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Calling it a dummymander is generous. This was more like moron-mandering.”

— A Republican strategist in Texas rues the dismal failure of Trump’s attempt to gerrymander the midterm elections.

HARD POWER: SRPSKA AT CPAC

Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik arrives at a voting station near Banja Luka on Oct. 4, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

Once sanctioned by the U.S. and the UK, Bosnia’s separatist Serb leader, Milorad Dodik, has lobbied himself into Washington’s good graces.

Dodik used to be president of Republika Srpska — a semi-autonomous, ethnic Serbian region of Bosnia — until last year, when he was stripped of his presidency and sentenced to a year in jail for defying the international envoy overseeing Bosnia’s peace accords. The U.S. and the UK sanctioned Dodik in 2022, accusing the ultra-nationalist politician of “corrupt activities” and threats to undermine the region’s stability and peace (he’s long pushed for Srpska to secede from Bosnia, a move that could reignite the region’s ethnic tensions).

But when Donald Trump returned to office, Dodik started to lobby his administration in hopes of earning diplomatic support from the president and getting his sanctions lifted. Dodik befriended Trump’s former personal lawyer, Rudy Giuliani — who visited Dodik in Srpska last year, donning a red “Make Srpska Great Again” cap while he appeared with the Serbian strongman at a rally. Giuliani also enlisted former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevichto lobby on behalf of Srpska.

Eventually, his advocacy campaign worked. The U.S. dropped the sanctions last year.

Since then, Dodik has only expanded his profile in Washington. Last month, he retained two of President Trump’s top political advisers as consultants ahead of last month’s general election. He thanked Trump when his party ultimately won the election, retaining power in the region:

“If it had not been for Donald Trump’s magnificent victory [in 2024] … we would probably be political corpses today,” he told supporters. “But now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners.”

And now, he’s earned himself a spot on Mar-a-Lago’s guest list. Dodik is joining MAGA’s top players this week at the CPAC Circle Retreat and Gala — an offshoot of CPAC, America’s annual confab for its far-right politicians, donors and allies — according to a report from the Atlantic, brushing shoulders with attendees like former British Prime Minister Liz Truss and failed Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

SOFT POWER: COLD PLAY

Russia is returning to the hockey rink — and the rest of the world is livid.

Russian sporting teams have been in exile since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The International Ice Hockey Federation, the International Olympic Committee, FIFA and Formula 1 have all banned or restricted Russian representation. But the Switzerland-based Court of Arbitration for Sport has ordered the IIHF to overturn their ban and reinstate Russian teams for the 2026-27 season, arguing that the hockey federation’s “safety, security and other concerns were not supported by sufficient evidence.”

The decision has thrown the hockey world into crisis. Hockey teams from Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Czech Republic and Latvia announced they will continue to refuse to play Russian teams. Two major sponsors of the Men’s World Championships, held next year in Germany, have threatened to pull out if Russia plays next year. Canada also will not welcome Russian players into the country for next month’s world junior championship, Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

“I thank Czechia, Denmark, Finland, Latvia, Norway and Sweden, and their national hockey federations, for publicly refusing to share the ice with Russia,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X. “Keep Russia off the ice! A war of aggression and hockey are incompatible.”

WEEKEND AGENDA

— President Trump to make a speech at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Friday.

— U.S. monthly jobs data released on Friday.

— Pope Leo XIV begins apostolic tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Friday.

— New Zealand to hold general election on Saturday.

Your daily briefing onSOUTH KOREA

Executive Briefing

South Korea adds future mine-clearance option to Cheonghae deployment plan

John Lee

South Korea advanced a proposal Thursday to expand the operating area of its Cheonghae anti-piracy unit from the Gulf of Aden to waters south of Oman, while increasing its authorized personnel from 320 to 395. The revised deployment plan would add a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft, an explosives disposal team and unmanned equipment for detecting and clearing naval mines. The expanded area would remain about 400 miles (650 kilometers) from the Strait of Hormuz.

The Ministry of National Defense said piracy had more than tripled as the Middle East conflict diverted naval resources, leaving commercial shipping more exposed. The proposal also adds restoring freedom of navigation to the unit’s objectives. The ministry stressed that South Korean forces would remain outside the U.S.-Iran war and confirmed that any future deployment to Hormuz would require separate National Assembly approval.

Big Tech & Startups

OpenAI launches Images 2.6 with GIFs and image reference (1 minute read)

OpenAI is rolling out Images 2.6 globally in ChatGPT and Codex. The new model generates images 50% faster than the previous iteration, and it can also create GIFs. Users can adjust the speed of GIFs, edit individual frames, and share them. GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst are now available through the API.

Apple Cuts Internal AI Usage Budgets in Move to Reduce Spending (5 minute read)

Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap on AI models for its employees last month. Some engineers had their budgets cut from $300 to $200, and the company is planning further cuts for some engineering teams that may potentially reduce their daily allowances to as little as $100. Groups outside of engineering may have their limits reduced to $25 from $100. Employees say that few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous.

Science & Futuristic Technology

SpaceX's Starfall just went from secret to storefront (16 minute read)

SpaceX has launched a commercial page for Starfall, a disk-shaped reentry capsule that can carry up to 1,000 kg of payload. The capsule can supply 1 kW of power and connect to the internet through Starlink, allowing researchers to pull data from experiments while in orbit instead of waiting for splashdown. It can be used for manufacturing, research, or testing and is aimed at biomedical customers, pharmaceutical companies, and materials science research. Starfall's timeline will depend on Starship - SpaceX is preparing for Flight 15, where it aims to catch both stages with the launch tower.

Why pharma firms are going to Earth's orbit in search of new cancer drugs (7 minute read)

Varda Space Industries' autonomous factories carry miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the process is complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft and returns to Earth. The company currently has three spacecraft simultaneously in orbit. Manufacturing in space has several advantages, one of the most important being microgravity. Varda plans to launch seven missions in 2027 and 10 in 2028.

Zero To Calc In Six Days: How AI Broke Chrome (Sponsor)

A Chrome full chain used to take six to nine months. XBOW's AI agents did it in six days for $40,000. Google paid the first $250,000 full-chain award. Every stage, and what it means for you.

Get the paper.

Rebuilding the global town square from scratch (32 minute read)

The new version of X.com's web app was built by five engineers working with AI coding agents in under six months. It loads pages significantly faster than the old web app over slow connections, and it already serves logged-out users and the pages that search engines crawl. This post covers why X.com was rebuilt, how the new web app is being rolled out, and how the old and new apps compare today. It also looks at the performance work completed since logged-out traffic moved over.

Fortune Telling and Speculative Design (21 minute read)

Design engineering requires being deeply involved in the technical craft and material of software. They help make decisions about functionality and architecture in code while still being a designer. Design engineers are uniquely positioned to make convincing prototypes of future theories. They are the perfect people to help figure out the shape of the future.

Miscellaneous

AI on the Ballot (18 minute read)

Nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning, with the exception of North Dakota. The constraint on AI dispersion is becoming political. AI will likely be a scarcity for much longer than expected. This post looks at what the implications might be if Americans don't change their minds about data centers.

Voice is Underutilized (6 minute read)

Voice is a natural modality that is underutilized. It is great for rambling at coding agents and for capturing context. There is a lot of ambient context that exists in conversations with a ton of downstream value. This post presents some use cases for voice as a way to interact with AI.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

Police investigates more rape allegations

The disgraced comedian has been remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday. Credit: Press Association

Russell Brand is being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women. This can now be reported following his conviction on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The 51-year-old faced seven charges over allegations dating from 1999 to 2009 made by six women. He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Our correspondent Sima Kotecha followed the three-week trial. She calls Brand's appearance in court "an extraordinary fall from grace" that bore little resemblance to the flamboyance most people may remember from the height of his fame.

AT THE SCENE

Johannesburg, South Africa

ANC under pressure in local elections

The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air in Alexandra. Credit: AFP via Getty Images

After voting on Wednesday, South Africa is waiting for the outcome of local elections that could see a haemorrhaging of support for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).

Khanyisile Ngcobo, BBC News

This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes. In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.

We met an 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so. But Sanele Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change. South of Johannesburg, Soweto looked marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents there complained about accessing water and electricity.

Hello. As the dust settles on the US midterms results, we explore the obstacles President Donald Trump may now face. Hungary has released its secret police files in a controversial move. And in Australia, a chef has been sacked after a row over pineapple on pizza.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

What the next two years could look like for Trump

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTEsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABt5BBvGAh35ih6XJD_-h0nySeSq8LGF36savOmLehcbh7f4iFj4vUpybYvlTH2uvk2XhBxTVEzc-eYu_nOI53JevZD9nZAnxkWc115o Some Republicans have criticised the president, something they would previously not have done. After bruising election results, Trump will want to show he is still "firmly in charge", writes North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher. While Democratic control of Congress will make life more difficult for the president, his executive authority and his ability to veto means he still wields power. BEYOND THE HEADLINES

Why Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTEsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABt5BBvGaEgLqZggELAGAC06gbFRz8BfvWpcnDWBymevs_OU8DVbbBPvSWhTK_26VMBFgkGAmjnRRlWa6ptxhrRrTP5QJoVdrNTAGc3Q More files are set to be released in February. Credit: Péter Magyar/Facebook

In a controversial move, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people who were recruited by Hungary's communist-era secret police have been released to the public. Between 1944 and 1990, around 150-160,000 people were recruited as informers, many through blackmail or coercion, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. The government says the files' release will help the country heal from the trauma of communist rule, but the move has sparked criticism.

The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference

Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA Working Nights & Weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Meta Muse Spark Open, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, SGLang, vLLM, llm-d, Ray

Bryan Shan, Alec Ibarra, Cam Quilici, Kimbo Chen, Wenyao Gao, Dylan Patel, and Myron Xie

Nov 5

Preview

READ IN APP

In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported.

Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy.

Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300.

We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading.

Today we are releasing long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result:

Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang).

GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss.

Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy.

Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by vLLM OSS ecosystem developer, Inferact.

This was benchmarked on InferenceX/AgentX, the industry-standard inference benchmark supported by almost every major buyer of compute, from Microsoft Azure to Oracle to Meta and many more. Furthermore, it has the support of the ML community, including vLLM, LMCache, SGLang, PyTorch, and Huggingface, and the support of major labs like OpenAI, MiniMax, ZAI, Qwen, Moonshot Kimi, etc.

Google potential TPU customers and current TPU customers are asking Google for AgentX results because of how realistic the AgentX benchmark is and how similar it is to their real inference workload. For our SemiAnalysis supply chain shipment estimates on TPUv8i, TPUv8t, TPUv9, TPUv10, check our Accelerator Model for full quarter by quarter breakdown of shipments.

Source: InferenceX

Star the InferenceX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful!. InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and soon, SambaNova and Trainium2/3.

Source: InferenceX

Recommendation to Jensen

NVIDIA only occasionally loses to AMD on some model/scenarios, but TPUs delivering better performance per dollar or competitive performance per dollar is a new experience that NVIDIA senior leadership is unwilling to accept. As soon as TPU posted its first AgentX result on Qwen3.5 397B FP8 showing that even TPUv7 FP8 could beat GB300 NVL72 FP4, NVIDIA tasked a strike force of human engineers and agent swarms to work 997, late into the night until 2am local time and on weekends, across USA and China. Unfortunately for NVIDIA, their first GB300 FP4 counter submission is still 1.64x worse per dollar than TPUv7 FP8 for external customers across most of the curve. We do think that with enough agent swarms, NVIDIA could regain a slight performance lead on GB300 NVL72 FP4 vs TPUv7 FP8, but on NVIDIA FP8 versus TPUv7 FP8, we believe that it is not possible for NVIDIA to regain SOTA for certain models.

One thing we hear a lot from open-source maintainers in PyTorch and NVIDIA customers is that there is a lot of bureaucracy; simple things, like adding a new feature to the NVIDIA driver to support a certain feature for PyTorch CudaGraph capture, have been stuck in “internal NVIDIA legal review” for three months. It makes little sense for lawyers to be the blocker for technical driver features. We have seen similar challenges when trying to get NVIDIA to add features like improving ConnectX, NVSwitch, HGX Board (Vulcan, Umbriel) DCGM power telemetry, where it takes a while just to get the timeline for the timeline. In comparison, startup mindset companies like AMD (under the leadership of Anush, Ramine, Vamsi, Lisa) can rapidly develop these features.

There needs to be an cultural shift in massively reducing bureaucracy at NVIDIA. This is one of the biggest risks to NVIDIA Moat that Jensen has to tackle. In our experience and many customers experience, Nvidia is now slower moving than AMD, Google, and Amazon to external suggestion, git commits, and feedback.

That being said, certain teams at NVIDIA are cutting through the bureaucracy, such as the NVIDIA ex-CentML vLLM team. AMD and TPUs added innovative Megakernel decode support to open source popular production inference engine. Within a week, they were able to defend the NVIDIA by rapidly adding and merging Megakernel support too (PR approved by AMD vLLM maintainer).

TPU is making big headway into the ecosystem, and multiple models, like Day 0 Meta’s Muse Spark Open support and Kimi K3.1 Pro already has day 0 TPU support, as it applies the NVIDIA playbook of giving open-source maintainers lots of chips. In contrast, NVIDIA’s contribution of clusters to community maintainers has increasingly been wrapped in DMV style bureaucracy and stingy at best. For a $5 trillion company, one would expect NVIDIA to be more liberal in contributing resources to OSS developers who work for free on improving the NVIDIA stack. We hope Jensen figures out how to eliminate the bureaucracy slowing progress.

In comparison, AMD has been increasingly less stingy and providing the upstream vLLM, TileRT, SGLang, Tokenspeed, etc. maintainers liberal access to clusters and rapdily increasing the CI fleet without miminal levels of bureaucracy.

Source: vLLM Dashboard

Meta’s Muse Spark Open FP4 816B on SGLang TorchTPU Agentic Inference Performance

Meta is one of the early adopters of TPU and is already deploying TPUv7 in production using SGLang-TorchTPU.

Source: Meta

Muse Spark Open is Meta’s latest 816B-parameter open model, and it is one of the launch models for SGLang-TorchTPU. On InferenceX’s agentic inference workload, a submission from RadixArk, a community developer and a lead maintainer of SGLang, shows that TPUv7 is competitive for decode performance per dollar even when using the cost basis of what Meta would pay when buying TPUs. For production inference, Meta uses SGLang for LLM inference and uses vLLM for RL training rollouts. When looking at end-to-end latency, TPUv7 still needs improvements to be competitive, such as continuing to optimize its prefill kernels. For decode kernels, TPUv7 SGLang is using a fully fused megakernel, which eliminates kernel launch latency. Furthermore, the submission uses SGLang HiCache CPU DRAM offloading using Google’s open-source, TPU native TPU-Sync library at high concurrency in order to improve prefix cache hit rates.

Source: SemiAnalysis & RadixArk

Note that Muse Spark Open is an extremely GPU-optimized model, and, in theory, not friendly to TPUs at all. This is due to Muse Spark Open’s 64 head dim, which means that for long-context attention, 25% of the systolic array is padded.

In comparison, GPU matrix cores consume small tiles, so a wide range of head dimensions, expert widths, and post-sharding KV head counts all land near peak. A dimension of 64 instead of 128 pays close to nothing on an H100 or a B200 and gets a cheaper attention layer for it. GPU architecture allowed researchers to prioritize evaluation performance without a loss in inference performance.

This is quite interesting as TPUs can get quite competitive performance on a model that is extremely unfriendly to TPUs. Note that AI labs with lots of TPU capacity, such as Anthropic and Google Deepmind and soon OpenAI, typically co-design their models such that the attention shapes would fit nicely on TPUs to avoid this issue.

Source: SemiAnalysis

When TPUs see model architecture with attention head_dim=256, they go full lambo mode.

Source: Mario Kart

Great work to the RadixArk team on this amazing achievement! They are actively working on updating the documentation such that everyone can get access to this optimized SGLang Muse Spark Open TPU configuration. We expect more AgentX results from RadixArk soon, showing that its SGLang-TorchTPU stack is production-ready.

GLM5.2 / 5.3 vLLM AgentX FP8 Agentic Inference Performance

GLM-5.2/5.3 is a frontier open model. It is an MoE transformer with 744B parameters and roughly 39B active per token. The model supports a 1M-token context through DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): a lightweight indexer scores prior tokens, and full attention runs over only the 2,048 selected tokens for each query.

For FP8, TPUv7 is the cheapest way to serve GLM-5.2 AgentX. From 60 to 300 tok/s/user, it delivers 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X at FP8, and 4.4x that of H200 at 150 tok/s/user.

Source: SemiAnalysis

FP4 GPUs Still Lead on Perf per Dollar

Because GLM-5.3 was not natively QAT with block scale FP4, FP4 has a slight accuracy drop compared to FP8. FP4 GPUs still deliver more tokens per dollar at most speeds, as TPUv7 has no native FP4 support, and we will need to wait until Q1 2027 for TPUv8 with FP4 support, as tracked in our Accelerator & HBM Model. At 100 tok/s/user, GB300 and GB200 FP4 deliver 3.6x and 3.5x the tokens per dollar of TPUv7. FP4 halves the bytes per weight, and small batch decode is memory bound.

Source: SemiAnalysis

The SemiAnalysis AI Cloud & TCO Model provides a comprehensive breakdown of pricing across all accelerators currently on InferenceX, as well as many more, including future SKUs such as Nvidia Rubin Ultra and Feynman, AMD MI400 through MI700, Google TPU v8 through v12, and AWS Trainium3 through Trainium6.

GLM-5.3 Optimizations

GLM-5.3 AgentX contexts reach 1M tokens with over 90% of each request already cached, so KV cache capacity sets how many users fit. There are four main changes:

GLM-5.3’s attention reads one shared compressed KV entry per token, so splitting attention heads across devices would copy the whole cache to every device. Decode context parallelism (DCP) splits it by sequence position instead and merges partial attention results every layer.

Source: SemiAnalysis & Google

Each query reads only the 2,048 cache entries an indexer selects. TPUv7’s SparseCores, built for scattered memory access, pick those entries and gather them while the TensorCore runs the attention math.

TPUv7 uses registers that are 8 rows by 128 lanes. Data must be packed into them, which can fragment. The 128 indexer key bytes plus the scale byte add up to 129, one byte more than a 128-wide row, so the old layout rounded it up to 256. The new layout turns it sideways: tokens now run along each row, and each token’s key runs down 32 four-byte rows, plus one more row for the scale. That comes to 132 bytes, and only 3 of them are wasted.

Source: SemiAnalysis & Google

One fused kernel runs routing; the experts, the all-reduce, and the attention merge become a single collective. TPU programs are compiled for fixed shapes, so Google added 4- and 8-token shapes for small decode steps, which had been padded to 16.

Qwen3.5 397B AgentX

Two weeks ago, Qwen3.5 397B became the first model Google submitted to AgentX. Its TPUv7 FP8 vLLM results on our agentic inference benchmark demonstrate that it is 1.67x better perf per dollar than even FP4 GB300 NVL72.

Source: SemiAnalysis

NVIDIA may try to claim that it doesn’t care about the Qwen3.5 397B model, but from analyzing our upstream InferenceX submission analytics datalake, the reality is that NVIDIA has spent over 20% of the sweep GPU hours on Qwen3.5 for certain NVIDIA GPU SKUs so it is hard for NVIDIA to claim that. In addition, if you look at the NVIDIA engineers assigned to Qwen3.5, it is some of the top 10x inference performance engineers at NVIDIA so clearly, NVIDIA cares about optimizing this model.

Furthermore, certain major hyperscalers/AI lab use Qwen3.5 397B and multi trillion parameter scale up version based on Qwen3.5 397B architecture as proxy models when making hardware purchasing and capacity planning decisions. So, this is a very important model for certain token factories.

For readers making purchasing decisions, our AI Cloud & TCO Model extends the analysis into cluster economics, including cash flow, investment returns, and accelerator residual values.

Get Access

AgentX captures the four elements of an agentic workload:

Multi-turn: a session includes many user / assistant interactions (tens or hundreds) compared to a handful in a chatbot scenario.

Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly.

High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n

Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KVCache patterns.

TPU was able to demonstrate that its upcoming TorchTPU vLLM stack can successfully handle agentic workloads.

Source: SemiAnalysis

NVIDIA First Counter Submission

NVIDIA engineers worked overtime to launch their counter submission FP4, which beats TPUv7 FP8 on decode performance, but there is a slight issue: they overtuned decode at the expense of prefill, hurting overall end-to-end performance. Thus, on end-to-end performance, TPUs FP8 is currently still beating GB300 NVL72 FP4.

Source: SemiAnalysis

Open Source Kubernetes llm-d puts TPUv7 far above GB300 FP8 for Decode Interactivity

Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate hosts so long prefills do not stall generation. llm-d is the open-source K8s router that coordinates them, each host is 4 TPUv7 chips, and each result uses 24-32 chips.

Source: SemiAnalysis

Speed comes from capping how many requests each decode host runs, from one at a time at the low-latency end up to 112 at the high-throughput end. Requests over the cap wait for a free host, which adds to their TTFT. Even so, p90 time to first token at the fastest point is 8.6 seconds, against 11.1 for GB300 FP4’s fastest point.

This uses llm-d, one of the largest ecosystem-based production inference kubernetes orchestrators. During the recent Kimi K3.1 Pro launch, they had Day 0 support for TPUv7 on llm-d.

Source: InferenceX

At FP8, TPUv7 with llm-d beats GB300 at every interactivity, from >2x at high throughput to achieving more than 1000tok/s/user in the ultrafast region.

Unfortunately, using this turn-based routing algorithm does lead to worse end-to-end performance for TPUs compared to GB300 TRTLLM FP4. However compared to FP8 and FP4 GB300 NVL72 SGLang, it is still much better.

Source: SemiAnalysis

Qwen3.5 TPU Optimizations

Qwen3.5-397B mixes 45 linear attention layers, which keep a fixed-size state per request, with 15 full attention layers. Google describes three main changes:

Decode megakernel. One kernel runs the whole decode step and prefetches the next layer’s weights while the current layer computes.

Host DRAM offload. KV cache and linear attention state spill to host DRAM through TPU Sync, Google’s newly open-sourced offload framework.

Cache-aware routing. llm-d sends each turn to the prefill host holding its prefix and keeps each session on its decode host unless that host is full. Google says routing to the exact data-parallel rank raised decode cache hit rates from 56% to 76%.

Kimi K3 AgentX

TPU from Inferact and AMD shipped megakernels for frontier MoE models first in open source engines. NVIDIA quickly followed within a week with its own megakernels.

A conventional decode step launches hundreds to thousands of kernels, and the chip idles between them. A megakernel runs many layers in one long-running kernel that prefetches the next weights, while the current ones compute. AMD calls its version the MonoKernel. On GLM-5.2 across eight MI350X GPUs, AMD reports that it cuts a decode step from about 2,459 launches to 210 and runs 2.31x faster at batch 1.

Source: SemiAnalysis

A megakernel removes the idle gaps between kernel launches. Read more about megakernels in our TileRT article:

Ultra-High Interactivity on NVIDIA GPUs? - TileRT InferenceX

Bryan Shan, Daniel Nishball, and 4 others

Aug 10

Read full story

For this setup, DCP was used for prefill. The prefill and decode variants of context parallelism describe where each technique usually helps, not where it can run. K3 uses MLA which stores KV as one latent shared across heads, so TP cannot split it and every TP rank holds a full copy. DCP fixes this by giving each TP rank a different slice of tokens. Prefill context parallelism would have needed a lower TP degree, which copies weights onto more chips and leaves less HBM for the KV cache, already the scarce resource here.

Source: Inferact

Competitive with GB300 FP4 at launch

At launch on October 17, TPUv7 delivered 0.77x to 0.91x GB300’s tokens per dollar from 50 to 200 tok/s/user and was 1.6x faster for a single user, at 391 tok/s/user against 251. On Google’s internal cost it beat GB300 at 100 and 200 tok/s/user.

Source: InferenceX

GB300 FP4 now leads by 1.5x to 2.6x after four NVIDIA refreshes. TPUv7 still delivers a competitive 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200 and B300, while VR200 delivers 4.3x to 5.6x TPUv7.

Source: InferenceX

In an apples to bananas comparison between TPUv7 & Rubin NVL72, Rubin is up to 6x better perf per dollar. But note that this is an unfair comparison as Rubin should be compared to TPUv8i which we will be benchmarking very soon.

Source: SemiAnalysis

Built by the Ecosystem

This result came from the vLLM ecosystem, not from Google alone. Inferact, founded by vLLM’s creators and maintainers, built the K3 megakernels with Google, and the two submitted the result together. The megakernel plugs into vLLM as a model runner that replaces only the forward, so vLLM’s scheduling, prefix caching and KV transfer work unchanged. The stack is open source on vLLM TorchTPU, and Inferact’s reproduction guide runs it from a Docker image. Ecosystem development like this has mostly happened on CUDA.

Source: Inferact...

Celine Touboul

Charting the Middle East

Prompted by the escalating risks facing civilians across the Gulf and Levant, governments and communities have strengthened warning systems to enhance public safety when conflict erupts. Yet, Saudi Arabia’s public warning systems fell silent ahead of the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab state since the start of the Iran war, raising concerns about the availability of timely warnings of incoming attacks. This installment of Charting the Middle East highlights the importance of early warning systems, emergency communications, and community-based warning mechanisms amid recurrent surges of conflict in the region.

Governments in the region are investing in the infrastructure needed to rapidly warn and evacuate residents when conflict spikes. Iran, Iraq, Jordan, and Kuwait adopted new mobile alert systems following the June 2025 12-day war and more recent regional escalations. Warning tones were adjusted in the UAE and Qatar after causing mass anxiety and stress. These systems provide timely warnings and information on the need to seek shelter, shielding residents from incoming threats. Other countries in the region, such as Lebanon and Syria, still lack a unified national warning system despite its exposure to prolonged conflict. If adequate systems were in place, more individuals may have access to life-saving information that could minimize casualty and injury rates, especially when attacks occur at night.

The expansion of early warning systems illustrates a broader shift in how regional governments are approaching conflict preparedness: protecting civilians increasingly depends not only on mitigating the effects of attacks, but on giving people enough information and resources to respond. With the persistent threat of a new escalation, the need for advanced early warning systems is more important than ever to minimize civilian harm in the region.

Headlines & Launches

OpenAI launches Images 2.6 with GIFs and image reference (1 minute read)

OpenAI is rolling out Images 2.6 globally in ChatGPT and Codex. The new model generates images 50% faster than the previous iteration, and it can also create GIFs. Users can adjust the speed of the GIF, edit individual frames, and share it. GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst are now available through the API.

Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 (5 minute read)

Pangram Image 1.0 is an AI image and AI video detection model that can produce a heatmap localizing exactly where AI appears in images. It is robust to edits, compression, and low resolutions. There is a Chrome Extension available that can detect AI, as well as API support for images and video.

Ripple-65B Preview (4 minute read)

Ripple-65B Preview is a frontier open-weight model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on TerminalBench 2.1. It surpasses significantly larger open-weight models from the US, including Reflection Beam 501B, Meta Muse Spark Open 816B, Thinking Machines Inkling 975B, and Nvidia Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B. The model was trained for only $32 million, one-tenth the estimated cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, and OpenRouter.

Deep Dives & Analysis

How OpenAI Patched 948 Linux Vulnerabilities (12 minute read)

OpenAI developed an autonomous pipeline for discovering, exploiting, and patching security vulnerabilities. In a single run, its cybersecurity model validated and generated patches for 948 Linux local privilege escalation vulnerabilities.

The Stacks Project, formalized in Lean (13 minute read)

Axiom has released a Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project. The Stacks project is an open-source reference that lays the foundation of modern algebraic geometry. The release is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built. It makes the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project available as a single, machine-checked library that researchers and AI agents can import from directly into new formal proofs.

Where Democrats Can Thwart Trump’s Foreign Policy

U.S. President Donald Trump has wielded the powers of the presidency like a sledgehammer during his second term—especially in foreign policy—and frequently bypassed Congress. From launching the Iran war and ordering strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats near Latin America, to the operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly taken major military action without congressional approval.

With Republicans controlling Congress in Trump’s second term so far, Democrats have been extremely limited in their capacity to challenge the White House on this and many other fronts. But that’s about to change. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with stunning upsets in races nationwide. This opens the door for Democrats to steer the United States in new directions on a range of key foreign policy issues after the new Congress is sworn in early next year.

Democrats will have control over the appropriations committees in both chambers and oversee the drafting of annual military and foreign aid spending bills. This far from guarantees that Democrats will get their way, but the power of the purse will grant them considerable influence and negotiating power...

For Ukrainians, U.S. Midterm Results Bring Some Hope

KYIV AND WASHINGTON—The outcome of the U.S. congressional elections this week, which gave Democrats control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will be welcomed in some countries more than others, including Ukraine—which has quarreled with Republican-controlled Washington off and on for two years now.

So what are ordinary Ukrainians saying about the results?

Access a paywall-free link.

The Beginning of the End of Trumpism

Americans have now delivered on what they’ve been telling pollsters all year: They’re mad as hell and they’re not going to take it anymore. In a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, voters have entrusted Democrats with both the House and the Senate, flipping their control simultaneously for only the fourth time in a midterm election since World War II. The reverses for the GOP include defeats in usually deep-red states such as Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas.

Trump is already distancing himself from the results—after encouraging voters to pretend he was on the ballot. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform, as he cast blame on the right-wing network Fox News for platforming Democratic party voices. But polls show that voters across the country were concerned about rising costs and government corruption as they cast their ballots on Tuesday. They also show that Americans were linking their dissatisfaction over those matters directly to Trump’s policies, including the Iran war and tariffs.

Democrats should, of course, take credit for running successful campaigns in states as different as Maine, Michigan, Nevada, and North Carolina. And they ran a diverse slate of candidates, from centrists such as Adam Hamilton, a pastor who has become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since the Great Depression, to Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, one of several new House representatives associated with the Democratic Socialists of America. But that broad tent—without a clear party leader or direction—suggests that the midterm vote was more a repudiation of the present than a roadmap for the future...

Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Midterms Wipeout

U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

It’s not often that a sitting vice president comes out so forcefully against a defining policy decision made by his boss—especially when that boss is as notorious for punishing perceived disloyalty as U.S. President Donald Trump is...

A (Chinese) burn

Tonight's edition also includes: Giorgia Meloni frustated over proliferation of diplomatic formats and initiatives

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Bruno Waterfield

Supported by

Hello, and welcome to Rapporteur PM.

China fired a shot across the EU’s bow today with a carefully scripted and weighted speech warning Brussels not to pull the trigger on “discriminatory” trade weapons to protect European industries.

In a rare speech, with printed-out copies distributed to an audience of officials and diplomats, Cai Run, China’s ambassador to the EU, delivered a clear warning to Europeans trying to stem the flow of Chinese imports.

His words at an event hosted by Friends of Europe, a Brussels-based think tank, could not have been clearer. Beijing does not accept the premise of new EU instruments crafted to curtail a trade deficit with China that amounts to €1 billion a day.

“China opposes politicising economic and trade issues, overstretching the concept of security, and resorting to unilateral or maximum pressure,” Cai said.

“If the EU insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory economic and trade measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests.

The message is a stark and simple one.

If the EU uses new trade defence weapons – and departs from the current soft strategy of “dialogue” with Beijing – then Europeans will have a fight on their hands.

Cai’s words throw down the gauntlet: does the EU have enough iron in its soul to slug it out with China, the world’s ascendant superpower?

As my colleague Thomas Møller-Nielsen has pointed out, it looks unlikely that the EU’s current crop of unpopular national leaders has the ability to “persuade their populations to bear the brunt of Chinese retaliation, especially at a time when the European economy is already suffering”.

Supported by Cement Europe

Europe’s waste has a place to go: cement kilns

Cement kilns turn waste with no other outlet into fuel and raw material: less imported fuel, fewer emissions, less landfill. The Circular Economy Act should build on routes that already work. See case studies from across Europe. Learn more here.

Round-up

BOMB THREATS: Over a dozen European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Thursday, following cyberattacks on supermarkets earlier this week. The European Commission said it was “too early” to determine whether a series of aircraft bomb hoaxes were linked or constituted a coordinated hybrid or cyberattack.

ITALIAN FRUSTRATIONS: Europe’s diplomatic disarray over Ukraine risks sidelining the EU in future peace negotiations, Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister, has warned. In a letter sent to António Costa, the president of the European Council, seen by Rapporteur, she expressed frustration at the proliferation of diplomatic formats and competing initiatives.

US DELUSIONS: A US push to make Europe buy more Russian gas would strengthen the Kremlin, harm America’s economy, and fail to end the war in Ukraine, Poland’s energy minister has warned. “If someone is deluding themselves by thinking they can buy time by buying Russian gas, it’s a very expensive and short-sighted game to play,” Miłosz Motyka said.

BETS ON BACKLASH: Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister, called for greater international cooperation with Latin American leaders as regional heads of state gathered at a Spanish summit, making thinly veiled references to a weakened US President Donald Trump. Sánchez is aiming to boost his international standing while facing problems at home, ahead of elections later this month.

READ TO ME

Welcome back to False Flag! What an election! If you’re anything like me and the Bulwark staff, it was a late night for you watching the returns come in. Pretty exciting stuff over here, but for the MAGA influencers who make up the False Flag menagerie, the tears weren’t happy ones. Tuesday’s dark night of loss has stretched on and on, turning into recriminations and bad blood over the party’s future.

As JVL says, happiness is when bad things happen to bad people. I don’t know about that, but what better way to keep track of the Republican party’s deeply miserable (and likely comical) new era than by joining Bulwark+? (Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Shutterstock)

THE POLLS HAD BEEN PREDICTING DOOM for his party for weeks, if not months. But as the first election results began rolling in on Tuesday afternoon, pro-Trump pundit Benny Johnson couldn’t help feeling good. Republicans had captured the governorship of Guam by 1,020 votes. Johnson, the right’s most prominent memester, told his fellow kids that control of the island—far closer to Papua New Guinea than to the continental United States—was a massively good omen for Republicans’ midterm hopes.

“An island that knows a lot about blue waves just went Republican!” he said.

The optimism didn’t last. Six hours after the big Guam win, as Democrats piled up electoral victories, Johnson was grimly intoning about the changing racial makeup of Texas. By Wednesday morning, with Democrats looking at a massive House sweep and a minimum of 54 Senate seats, he could no longer pretend Guam was significant at all.

“What happened last night was a meteor strike and an unmitigated disaster,” he said.

By Wednesday evening, having obsessively posted and livestreamed about the election for twenty-four hours, he professed emotional indifference to it all. “Notice how you don’t see any videos of Republicans bursting into tears, weeping and hysterical on social media after the loss?” he declared. “That’s because we have more to live for than party politics.”

Johnson wasn’t alone on his emotional rollercoaster. After seeing their party badly blow the midterms, conservative personalities are currently struggling to process the defeat. Delusion has become disbelief. Disbelief has become despair. And despair has become disgruntlement. Along the way, they are turning on one another.

On Piers Morgan’s election stream, anti-Israel libertarian comedian Dave Smith accused right-wing personality Jack Posobiec of misleading Republicans about the chances of a peace deal with Iran, prompting a tense on-air clash between the two.

On the Daily Wire’s livestream, podcaster Matt Walsh said of the war in Iran that he would have preferred that Iran develop a nuclear bomb if that meant preventing a “Communist” victory in the midterms. The claim amounts to a serious difference of opinion with hawkish Daily Wire boss Ben Shapiro.¹

Meanwhile, anti-DEI activist James Lindsay, who has become an opponent of the Israel foes, groypers, and antisemites—whom he has collectively dubbed the “Woke Right”—called for his enemies to be purged from conservative institutions.

So much for free speech!

A MESSAGE FROM OUR SPONSOR CLIMATE POWER

Data Center Download

In every 2026 race where data centers were central—Democrats won. Out of 41 ballot measures to rein in data center development, only one failed. Trump and Republicans paved the way for dirty data centers, causing energy prices to soar and harmful pollution. Voters are clear: They aren’t on board.

RIGHT-WING MEDIA has always been a fractious place even under the best of circumstances, featuring combustible personalities with flexible ethical standards clashing with one another in the pursuit of influence, followers, and money. A civil war has roiled the podcast right for over a year, turning intertwined issues like the Epstein files, Charlie Kirk’s murder, and the Iran war into the stuff of both conspiracies and blood feuds.

But the midterm rout, which none of these folks seemed to see coming, has cranked the stakes up to eleven. That’s partially because right-wing media figures are worried about their future. If no one wants to be a Republican anymore, who’s going to watch their podcasts and buy their brain pills? But it’s also because there’s a genuine belief that the fate of their ideological projects is at stake.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr., two figures tied to the Iran war by their proximity to Trump, also took the dramatic step of blaming the midterm losses on the war. And they weren’t the only prominent Republicans trying to create distance between themselves and the electoral catastrophe.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, now positioning himself as the country’s leading 2028 Republican and blameless for the war, said the midterms had been a near “extinction-level event” for the GOP.

In the past, fickle as he is, Trump could have acted as a pillar of order for conservative media: Get in line behind him or lose your White House access and audience. But with Trump inexplicably choosing to spend the election aftermath on Wednesday touring the under-construction White House ballroom, shellshocked Republicans ran wild. Even Brilyn Hollyhand, the Charlie Kirk knockoff who rose to a small level of prominence after Kirk’s assassination, criticized Trump for blowing a chance to rally the party.

So too did Walsh, who posted of the ballroom event, in which Trump seemed childishly gleeful watching beams being pulled by cranes: “This is far worse than I anticipated.”

Still, most MAGA influencers proved not quite ready to criticize Trump directly, which led them to spin bizarre theories about what could have really resonated with independent voters. As an example, podcaster Liz Wheeler said Republicans would have won if only the Justice Department had arrested more deep-state operatives from the Biden administration.

Surely that would’ve saved Kansas!

AMONG ALL THE HORRIBLE developments for Republicans that took place Tuesday night, perhaps the most alarming for online MAGA was the collapse of Texas Republican candidates. The state has been a bastion of the modern conservative movement, not just reliably red and with leadership willing to gerrymander the shit out of congressional lines, but also the right’s favorite contrast to hedonistic California.

So when it became clear that Democrats were romping there, it led to an onslaught of white identity politics that could make the movement even more radioactive to voters. Like Johnson, personalities at the Blaze blamed nonwhite voters for sabotaging the Texas GOP.

“Why import people you know are going to routinely vote against you?” asked the Blaze pundit who uses the alias “Auron MacIntyre.”

As always, no one was doing it with quite as much bigoted panache as Trump devotee Laura Loomer, who tweeted that Americans should start learning Arabic to prepare for our impending Islamic takeover.

Loomer’s meltdown over the midterms included far more than mere racial animus. While she watched the results come in Tuesday, she posted on X that Trump’s America250 celebrations were an early funeral for the American dream and that she may have lost her faith in God.

Loomer continued to grapple with the results at an existential level on Wednesday morning. Reflecting on the vote, she tweeted that the elderly were the “bigger winners” of the night. Why? Because they’ll die soon.

“They won’t have to see the collapse of America,” she said. She, on the other hand, will have to live through it all.

This robotics concept helps explain the jaggedness of frontier capabilities

Sim-to-real gaps are everywhere.

Timothy B. Lee

Nov 5

Preview

READ IN APP

The last year has seen incredible progress in model capabilities in certain domains — most notably programming, mathematics, and cybersecurity. Yet the real-world impact of these breakthroughs has been surprisingly modest — especially outside of those professions.

Lawyers, architects, salespeople, college professors, and others are certainly using AI models in their work, but AI models don’t seem close to transforming those professions the way they seem to be transforming mathematics and computer programming. And even in the software industry, we’re not seeing the kind of mass unemployment many people expected we would see once AI models reached human capabilities.

A big question is why — and whether the impact might grow in the next few months or years. Many people expect massive AI-driven disruptions to begin hitting other professions in 2028 or even 2027.

I don’t think that’s going to happen, and a concept from robotics helps to explain why: the sim-to-real gap. I encountered this concept when I was editing my colleague Kai Williams’s excellent September article about the scramble to collect robotics training data.

Suppose you want to train a robot to walk. One option is to create a virtual environment with a simulated robot. Then use reinforcement learning to reward behaviors that help the robot move around. The robotics startup Figure used this strategy last year and it worked! Figure said that it collected “years worth of simulated demonstrations in a few hours.” When they transferred the trained model to a real robot, the robot was able to walk “with no tweaks or changes.”

But this strategy doesn’t work as well for many other tasks. Kai gave an example where researchers tried to teach a robot to hammer a nail in simulation. The middle panel shows what happens if the robot tries to learn this task purely through trial and error:

A clip of different robot policies controlling a simulated hand, from Learning Complex Dexterous Manipulation with Deep Reinforcement Learning and Demonstrations (2017). The reinforcement learning policy (center) grips the simulated hammer awkwardly compared to either a human-controlled demo (left) or the policy trained with the paper’s method that mixed demonstration data and reinforcement learning (right).

Why does simulation work for walking but not hammering? A key difference, as Bracket Bot CEO Brian Machado explained to Kai, is that “the floor doesn’t do anything.” Because the floor is a static object that doesn’t change in response to a robot’s actions, it’s very easy to simulate.

A hammer isn’t as easy to simulate. You need to account for all of the forces and frictions between the hammer and the hand. If the simulation is even slightly inaccurate, the model might learn a hammering technique that works in simulation but fails in the real world.

Most economically valuable robotics tasks are more like hammering than walking. They require robots to manipulate objects that behave in complex, hard-to-simulate ways. Think, for example, about a rope, a half-full glass of wine, or a balloon. We don’t know how to simulate objects like these with enough fidelity to train a robotics model. And we really don’t know how to simulate the far more complex behavior of people and animals.

This has big implications for the future of robotics. If a task can be simulated, then a company can collect “years worth of simulated demonstrations in a few hours,” as Figure did when it was training its robots to walk. Robot performance can be improved rapidly at low cost.

But if simulation isn’t an option, then companies are left with much less appealing choices. They can hire humans to generate training data — either by teleoperating a robot or performing tasks themselves — and then use that data to train a robot. Or they can deploy a robot that doesn’t yet work very well and have it improve by trial and error.

Each of these approaches has its advantages and downsides. But all of them are much slower and more expensive than training in simulation. And this is a major reason I — and many robotics experts — are skeptical that general-purpose robots will be ready for widespread commercial deployment in the next few years.

AI companies face similar difficulties outside of robotics. You might think that white-collar work doesn’t suffer from a sim-to-real gap because it mostly happens on computers. But I think that’s wrong. Almost every white-collar profession involves interacting with other people and the larger world — which is almost impossible to simulate. And this fact limits how quickly AI models can replace human workers in these professions.

Math and coding are easy to simulate

In 2016, a DeepMind model called AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol, one of the world’s best human Go players. Soon afterwards, DeepMind developed AlphaZero, a more powerful successor that achieved superhuman performance at Go (as well as chess and shogi) by playing millions of games against itself.

You can think of Go and chess as tasks with very small sim-to-real gaps. AlphaZero’s self-play is reminiscent of Figure’s virtual robots teaching themselves to walk in simulation. And as with Figure’s virtual robots, the skills AlphaZero learned in training transferred well to “real-world” games against human beings.¹

Something similar has been happening in programming. Over the last 18 months, coding agents have revolutionized the programming profession. Instead of writing code themselves, programmers increasingly describe the code they want and rely on coding agents to generate it.

Here too, rapid progress has been made possible by a very small sim-to-real gap. Like Go, programming languages like Python and JavaScript have precise rules defining exactly how any given program should operate. This means that if LLMs hone their programming skills in a training environment, the skills they learn will transfer well to “real” programming tasks.

So too in mathematics. Four years ago, LLMs struggled with basic arithmetic. This year, frontier models have solved some of the discipline’s hardest problems.

Once again, this has been enabled by a minimal sim-to-real gap. A key move has been to use Lean, a language that allows mathematical proofs to be stated precisely and then verified automatically. This effectively turns mathematical reasoning into a computer programming task; frontier labs can automatically check whether a model has produced a valid proof for a particular problem. A proof that can be written in Lean is likely to be accepted by human mathematicians as well.

In short, we know how to train an AI model to achieve superhuman performance on a task if we can replicate that task in a training environment. In robotics, that describes locomotion tasks like running, jumping, and dancing — but not manipulation tasks like folding a T-shirt or painting a wall. Outside of robotics, games like chess and Go are easy to simulate. So are intellectual tasks like programming and proving mathematical theorems.

A crucial question for the AI industry is whether similar training techniques will work for other white-collar professions. Last year, OpenAI announced GDPval, a benchmark designed to measure the performance of frontier models in domains like mechanical engineering, social work, and real estate. In this benchmark, a model is given a PDF, spreadsheet, or other document describing a task and is asked to produce a new document in response. For example, given a spreadsheet of recent purchase orders at a company, a model might be asked to generate a new spreadsheet listing likely data entry errors.

Frontier labs hope they can train AI models to perform these kinds of cognitive tasks as effectively as they write computer code. And models have made significant progress on GDPval. When the benchmark was released a year ago, the best model, Claude Opus 4.1, got 47.6%. Today’s best models are scoring more than 85%.²

So are we about to see AI agents overrun finance and law and social work and architecture and mechanical engineering in 2027 the way they overran software engineering in 2026? I’m skeptical. And the concept of sim-to-real gaps helps to explain why...

Daily Memo: Russia-Sudan Talks, North Korean Naval Power

Today's Updates from Geopolitical Futures

Daily Memo: Russia-Sudan Talks, North Korean Naval Power

By: Geopolitical Futures - November 4, 2026

New plan. Sudan has reportedly reopened negotiations with Russia over a strategic foothold on the Red Sea, proposing a free economic zone that could host Russian logistics facilities while avoiding some of the political sensitivities surrounding a formal naval base. The new proposal emerged during talks around last week’s Russia-Africa Summit, where a senior Sudanese delegation also sought Russian drones, air defense systems, ammunition and spare parts in exchange for concessions in gold, copper and other minerals. The discussions have reignited a 2020 agreement on a Russian naval facility that was never fully implemented and could have given Moscow its first permanent naval foothold in Africa overlooking one of the world’s most important shipping corridors.

Why it matters: The negotiations highlight the increasingly transactional relationship between Russia and the Sudanese government, linking military support and diplomatic backing with access to minerals and strategic infrastructure on the Red Sea.

Naval power. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspected progress on the Nampo shipyard modernization project and construction of a new warship, state media reported. He was briefed on the plan to remodel the site and said the need to bolster the navy’s combat capabilities “stems from the emerging new geopolitical situation and the need to suppress by force the nuclear blackmail and threats of regional adversaries that are having a substantial and grave impact on national security.”

Why it matters: The upgrade will help North Korea build and repair more warships, supporting its effort to expand sea-based missile forces. Stronger North Korean naval capabilities will increase surveillance and defense requirements for South Korea, Japan and the United States. Sustaining and protecting these ships against superior air and naval forces will constrain how effectively North Korea can use its growing fleet.

Read More of Our Latest Analysis

Chinese engagement. Chinese authorities are open to dialogue with Iran, Saudi Arabia and other countries on preventing the resumption of conflict in the Middle East, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. The representative added that Beijing would maintain an “objective and impartial stance” and support efforts to resolve the conflict between Iran and the U.S., find a political solution to the crisis in Yemen and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Why it matters: China depends on energy resources that normally flow through Hormuz but has continued to support Iran throughout the war and Hormuz closure. At the same time, tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia have put Beijing, which is allied with both, in a difficult position.

Turkey and the UAE. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with senior UAE officials in Abu Dhabi to discuss regional security. The UAE’s vice president, national security adviser and secretary-general of the Supreme Council for National Security attended the meeting.

Why it matters: Ankara is reaching out simultaneously to several regional players to address regional challenges.

Defense ties. Syrian Defense Minister Murhaf Abu Qasra met with the Pakistani military attache to Damascus and Baghdad. They discussed prospects for cooperation and strengthening military ties between the two countries.

Why it matters: The meeting came just days after the Syrian foreign minister said his country was considering joining the Mecca joint defense pact, which comprises Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
