Trump Retreats to His Happy Place

by Andrew Egger

It’s tough on the chattering class, living through a major political sea change. After Trump’s shocking win in 2016, pundits were suddenly deprived of the stores of political wisdom they’d spent years accumulating. Who could say how it had happened, or what would come next? Like everybody else, the analysts were groping blindly in the dark. (They compensated by visiting diners in rural Ohio to talk to voters.)

Right now feels a bit like that too. Up until Tuesday night, the Trump era had been defined by certain rules. You could count on Trump always to do the most self-serving thing, to drag his party along with him, to ruthlessly quash dissent. And from about 2018 on, you could typically count on the GOP to go along with this arrangement.

Are these still the rules after the midterm shellacking? Can Trump continue his generational run as Republican god-emperor? Here’s an even more astonishing question: Is he even going to try?

Yesterday, as the Republican blame game got going, Trump wasn’t the one laying out the case for how the GOP could regroup and recover. That job fell instead to Vice President JD Vance. And remarkably, the case Vance made was one more in keeping with his own views than with his own administration’s party line. In a long treatise on X, Trump’s veep laid out the ways his own administration had brought calamity upon itself.

“There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is,” Vance wrote. “But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. . . . The reason we lost is the war.”

To woo back the voters they lost, Vance argued, the administration would need to end the Iran war, refocus itself on cost-of-living issues, put America first, and “change our relationship to Israel.”

This would be extraordinary stuff from any vice president—let alone Trump’s, with his mobland obsession with personal loyalty. Vance has found plenty of ways this year to get the word out about his own reservations about the Iran war. But this is the first time he’s said fuck it and just started posting on main. And why not? What has he got to lose? Vance’s odds of winning the presidency in 2028 have never been lower, and even he must see that there’s certainly no path there anymore as Donald Trump’s Bestest Little Guy. Of course, it doesn’t seem very likely to work: There’s only so much you can do to distance yourself from a White House when you’re its second-in-command. And you can only bemoan so much about the need to end the war when you led the negotiations that failed to end it.

Trump be losing friends and influence throughout the Republican party, keep the pressure up and join us at The Bulwark.

Join

Vance was hardly the only Republican trying to chart a path forward. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, whose state Republicans weathered the blue hurricane better than most, spent yesterday repeatedly offering grim assessments of the dead-end trajectory of the current party and the opportunities it had squandered to get here. MAGA dissidents like Tucker Carlson were happy to twist the knife, too: “We can say, without hyperbole or gloating, this is the end of the Trump era last night,” Carlson said on his show. “We’re done.”

Even replacement-level GOP senators found their tongues for what felt like the first time in years. “Look, the president made it very clear that he was on the ballot,” South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds, who was re-elected this week, told a local news station. “I think he did a lot of things right. But I think there were some challenges in the way some of those were executed. . . . We’re also going to have to take a second look at some of the executive branch decisions that have been made.”

The most incredible thing about all this wasn’t just that it seemed to happen independent of Trump himself. It was how little Trump even seemed to care.

All around him, his party was feverishly planning for a future that barely seemed to involve him. In some cases, a future that seemed organized against him. Meanwhile, he spent yesterday retreating further up his own ass. Hours after Vance posted his manifesto, Trump hurriedly assembled reporters to treat them—I swear I am not making this up—to fifteen minutes of aimless chitchat about his new East Wing ballroom.

“It’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years,” Trump said. “You could put as many helicopters as you want on the roof.”

Eventually, Trump took some questions about the election, including whether he’s worried about being impeached—“what, for having a successful country?”—but he quickly tired of them. “Watch the beam go up,” he ordered the press. “Now envision chandeliers.”

You have to imagine Trump will not stay quite this dissociated forever. He has plenty of reasons to lock back in: A world where he doesn’t rule his party with an iron fist is a far less pleasant one for him going forward, one with far fewer opportunities to rake in the benjamins and far more legal storm clouds on the horizon.

But for now, at least, we are seeing something that would have seemed unimaginable just a few days ago. For a decade, the GOP has been a solar system that revolves around one supermassive star. Yesterday, we got a glimpse of what it will look like when that star suddenly goes out.

Blue, eh?

by Martyn Wendell Jones

Toronto, Ontario

Considering the threats, tariffs, and mockery President Donald Trump has directed at Canada over the last two years, one might expect Canadians to be positively thrilled with the drubbing the Republicans took in the midterm elections. But so far, north of the border, reactions have been a bit more circumspect.

“Yes, the Republicans took a pounding—by recent American standards,” wrote Globe and Mail columnist Andrew Coyne, one of the paper’s more conservative voices. But the 41 or 42 percent of the popular vote he expected Republicans to pick up in the final count “would exceed the winning party’s vote share in most recent Canadian elections,” and therefore he found it difficult to view the result as the thoroughgoing repudiation of Trump’s deranged politics that many Americans have taken it to be.

The fact that “tens of millions of Americans continue to support him,” Coyne wrote, is “as much the lesson of this election as the Republican losses.”

In a similar vein, Toronto Star columnist Justin Ling characterized the blue wave that put Congress firmly in the hands of the Democrats as a “productive cough for democracy in the United States.” But like Coyne, he bemoaned the lack of a supermajority in either chamber that could otherwise enable Democrats to override Trump’s veto power, which the president has threatened to deploy in various interviews and taunted his opponents with in a Truth Social post.

Ling expects Trump to befuddle Congress through the sort of thin-slicing “salami tactics” the Communist Party used to consolidate its rule in post-war Hungary. As for what Canadian leadership should do about it, he thought it would be “mad” to accept a new trade deal with the U.S. under Trump—arguing that Prime Minister Mark Carney should stay the course and continue to watch Canada’s non-U.S.-bound exports grow.

Journalist Matt Gurney said he hopes Americans have a shot at stabilizing their political situation, but expects that “most damage won’t be reversed.” And not only that.

“U.S. voters would inflict more of the last two years on the Western allies in a heartbeat for cheaper gas and ground beef,” he lamented.

Such dour assessments underscore a harsh reality about Trump’s second term: It’s going to be years before erstwhile international allies, Canadians among them, become open to re-establishing the friendly, easygoing relationship they once enjoyed with the United States. One former U.S. ambassador to Canada called for Congress to begin “a formal reconciliation process with Canada . . . almost the first day they come into office in January.” That could offer a good first step—but the collective foot of Democratic lawmakers will hang in the air without finding a place to put down if Trump continues making noise about Canadian annexation, as he did at rally appearances in the lead-up to the midterms. Members of his cabinet cheered on the cause of Albertan secession. And just days before Americans went to the polls, the current U.S. ambassador to Canada suggested the country could be blamed for unfavorable midterm results for Republicans owing to the role he expected trade pressures to play in key border states.

Even prominent Democrats have acted in ways that have alienated the Canadian public. On October 14, five days before Alberta’s independence referendum, Sen. Adam Schiff visited the province and met with Premier Danielle Smith—a right-wing figure many Canadians criticize for her role in the separatism crisis—to discuss trade issues. During an interview back in August, California Gov. Gavin Newsom was reluctant to commit to reversing Trump’s tariffs against Canada. (He has since come around.) Many Canadians took these acts for evidence that Canada won’t necessarily be better off under a Democratic administration than a Republican one. Something fundamental has changed.

Many Americans profess to love and respect Canada and see Trump’s actions, such as “renaming” Lake Ontario, as ridiculous and demeaning. Canadians have interpreted Trump’s belligerence differently: as a threat to their sovereignty. They are correct to do so. Canada’s economy was struggling even before Trump’s latest round of tariffs went into effect; one CBC reporter estimated that the 50 percent duties Trump imposed on $28 billion of Canadian exports in late August put tens of thousands of jobs and half a point of the country’s GDP freshly at risk.

To many on both sides of the border, the midterms betoken a light at the end of the authoritarian tunnel in the United States. But we Americans need to find our way out ourselves before we can expect to approach our former friends with tidings of normality. For now, we continue to travel in the dark.

QUICK HITS

HEGSETH ON THE HOT SEAT: Republicans may be more willing than before to fault Trump for their party’s disastrous year. But it’s plain that the party is still eager to find fall guys to blame where they can—and as CNN reports, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is first on the list:

Many Republican lawmakers and allies alarmed by Tuesday’s wipeout are moving swiftly to pin blame for the election results on Hegseth, arguing behind the scenes that he played a chief role in convincing Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy—and no plan for managing the inevitable political fallout. . . .

Hegseth, a vocal cheerleader for the war, oversold the US’ ability to win the conflict quickly and easily, multiple Republicans argued to CNN, describing on condition of anonymity why many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary. They accused him of continuing to advocate for escalation despite little sign that continued bombing has brought Iran closer to surrender.

How bad has it gotten? Rep. Thomas Massie says he plans to force a vote to impeach Hegseth next week—and multiple Republican sources told CNN they expect it to pass. Read the whole thing.

WILL MAHA STAY WITH MAGA?: Another possible casualty of Tuesday’s wipeout: The MAGA–MAHA alliance. Politico reports that Democrats are gearing up to court Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health-conscious followers, just as many in that group have soured on the White House’s agribusiness-friendly policy agenda:

The union two years ago of Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement and Donald Trump’s MAGA legions was one of convenience. Trump wanted to defeat Kamala Harris. Kennedy got a chance to pursue food, agriculture and vaccine policies that would have been anathema in earlier eras of Republican politics.

This week’s losses have thrown that calculus into doubt, raising questions about whether the energy that brought MAHA and MAGA together can sustain the coalition into 2028—and whether Republicans have sufficiently engaged the voters that helped them elect Trump in 2024.

“I hope every single politician is reminded that they didn’t buy these voters, they rented them. The voters have said they’re moving, and they haven’t necessarily moved to the Democrats. The Democrats are going to have to earn it,” said Tiffany Cianci, an online influencer who did volunteer work for Kennedy’s presidential campaign and identifies as an unaffiliated voter.

TUTORIAL

How to build an on-demand data analyst for your team with Grok Bot

Photo: @bot on X

Open Grok Bot > click ‘+’ > Create a Bot and create a dedicated Bot for company data analysis.

Open the Bot’s settings and connect the data sources, files, plugins, and credentials it needs to access your company data.

Add any company-specific context it should follow, such as metric definitions, table descriptions, reporting rules, and dashboard conventions.

Sample Prompt: “Act as our company data scientist. Investigate [metric/question] using our connected data. Query the relevant tables, check the result by [segment/time period/region], identify the most likely drivers, flag data-quality issues, and return a concise explanation with supporting charts and the exact metrics used.”

Run several real queries, review its analysis, and update the Bot’s instructions or add a ‘Skill’ for any recurring analysis workflow.

Open ‘Share’ > ‘Publish to Team’, then choose whether to publish the Bot with its existing context or start the shared version fresh.

Teammates can then open it from ‘Team Bots’ or use the connected Slack integration to ask data questions on demand.

FROM THE FRONTIER

Personal agents might be the subscription economy’s worst nightmare

Made with Midjourney

Agents are coming for the laziness tax. Many companies profit from customer inertia. Gyms often make canceling a nightmare, insurance providers auto-renew at higher rates, and streaming services subtly double prices through steady hikes you barely notice. Most people know they’re overpaying but just can’t be bothered to cancel every account. Agents can.

Tech leaders are pitching agents as money savers

Personal agents are quickly finding a niche: handling chores everyone wants done, but nobody has time to do.

Meta’s Alexandr Wang has highlighted many cases of Muse saving customers money by haggling bills, including this thread.

After a wave of updates, Grok Bot seems custom-built for canceling subscriptions. It can even call companies directly to cancel services, with a recent demo video showing it pushing back against a customer service rep.

Agents could even shake up banking. JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo hold about $1.6T in deposits paying no interest, while high-yield accounts offer up to 5%. Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, has already warned that we may see an agentic bank run if enough customers use their agent to optimize returns.

The list goes on: software tools, cell phone plans, free trials, credit cards, utilities. Agents will save customers time and money, but may upend entire industries along the way.

Craft and taste

What does old me think

Ben Tossell

Nov 5

READ IN APP

As I’m exploring what truly interests me, there’s something that’s getting clearer as the days go by. Something that I keep peeking at through the trees.

I value taste.

And I know that’s an overused term these days, plus it’s different for everyone else but I can just feel what I like and don’t like. It flows from products I use, to what I wear, to the founders I invest in. Maybe there’s some built up instinct from running the Product Hunt homepage for 2 years back in 2015 and combing through tens of thousands of products.

Taste is the reason why I can’t do things that are not authentic to me. I refuse to tweet ‘for growth’. I turn down acquisitions or job offers.

So I wanted to see what past me and current me really like.

I asked Codex to pull my history from Kindle and Spotify to see if my feeling of this ‘thing’ was true. What have I been consuming for hours just for fun, just because I find it interesting?

Books and podcasts feel like a strong signal because I’ve paid for it and/or spent hours in it. I also pulled my YouTube history and Readwise articles/newsletters but I don’t think 885 videos of The Wiggles shows me anything other than being a parent…So I focused mostly on books.

With the data all in a folder I got Opus 5.5 to show me what my consumption looked like.

Then I asked Opus to try a few different agents with no context to look at the data to see what it thinks my interests are.

Kinda…

But what it re-affirmed to me was more nuanced than that… It’s not just ‘business’ books or founders’ stories that I like. It’s the how. How did this person or company do this thing? Why people made choices that others didn’t? What alternative path did they take and succeed?

I’ve been diving into David Senra recently - mostly interviews on him as the subject (he reads autobiographies of founders and does a podcast on them). I resonate a lot with how he thinks about his own ‘work’. One big thing that keeps sticking with me is stories sell products.

It’s taste. It’s uniqueness. It’s values. It’s going against the grain. Doing something different.

For example, I use Granola because I like the founders, the company, their values, their vibe, their taste and of course, their product. Sure there’s a ton of competitors but its the care of their craft that I really feel. So I pick them over others. I don’t see the Granola founders ever going on youtube to do this kind of stuff.

yes this is the founder of wispr flow talking about himself being a ‘$2b startup ceo’

I get we’re in an attention game but this feels icky to me.

I buy clothes from Kith because I know a lot about the founder and how he think about his brand (plus I loved streetwear growing up). Its an extension of him and what he likes. Great Senra interview with him here btw that I found this morning.

There’s a ton of companies and builders out there who do or have done something differently. Just because its authentically them. Those are the products I want to buy. And those are the stories that interest me.

So I’m going to be looking into those stories and building interactive sites, some with video, some with behind the scenes of my process. That is what I’m going to focus on doing.

The ‘how we make money’ isn’t something on my mind to figure out yet. If I focus on tasteful builders I’m sure companies would want to be part of that narrative but it allows me to make my own judgement on whether I’d even want to do something with them.

I feel like if the format is interesting enough, it can make you care about the topic (even if you think you won’t) - which is why I love the interactive essays by The Pudding. I don’t care about women’s jean pocket sizes, but you bet I read the essay because I love the format.

That’s the kind of feeling I want.

Oh and I turned my book history into a scrollable timeline for fun.

Quick bites

ChatGPT Images 2.6 - faster, better and now with GIFs

Reverse engineering TikTok - they know if you’re lying down, walking or in a car

Pivoting to focus on fun.

Notion is ‘reinventing itself’ - context for agents.

Agent experience is the new user experience.

Hello!

Today: Will the political backlash against data centers derail Texas’s AI ambitions? Plus: How the midterms could reshape US energy policy, and the Senate's vote on a new bill next week that aims to speed up the approval of energy infrastructure projects.

Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.

Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.

The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.

Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future.

—James O'Donnell

What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?

Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.

The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.

Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy.

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure

A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.

Explore the trade-offs behind America's proposed permitting overhaul.

—Casey Crownhart

One more thing

Meet the radio-obsessed civilian shaping Ukraine’s drone defense

Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov is, at least unofficially, a spy. Once a month, he drives to the frontline in a VW van equipped with radio hardware, roof antennas, and devices that monitor drones. Over several days, he searches the skies for transmissions that can help Ukrainian troops.

Drones define this brutal conflict, and most rely on the radio communications Flash has obsessed over since childhood. Though now a civilian, the former officer has taken it upon himself to inform his country’s defense on all matters related to radio.

Unlike traditional spies, Flash shares his discoveries with over 127,000 followers—including soldiers and officials—on social media. His work has won fans in the military, but also sparked controversy among the top brass. Read the full story.

—Charlie Metcalfe

The New Senators on China

Fresh faces in the Villa!

Jordan Schneider, Lily Ottinger, Aqib Zakaria, Quinn Ennis, and Irene Zhang

Nov 5

READ IN APP

Voters showed up in historic fashion for the Democrats on Tuesday night, flipping control of both houses and leaving Trump a lame duck for his final two years. These races were won mostly by campaigning on affordability and corruption.

But you’re ChinaTalk readers! So what did this new crop of legislators have to say about China? What kind of fresh takes does the Senate class of 2027 bring to the table on chip controls, AI competition, and, uh, Chinese shrimp?

We selected 12 senators to highlight here. Read on to learn about:

Abdul El-Sayed’s thoughts on compute restrictions;

Why seafood makes Julia Letlow a China Hawk;

Chris Pappas’ fixation with Taiwan;

Whether Peggy Flanagan is AGI-pilled;

And Mississippi’s first-ever election ad in Mandarin…

Abdul El-Sayed (D) — MI

Jordan: Abdul El-Sayed, the 42-year-old senator-elect from Michigan, is the rare breed of Sanders-esque China dove who isn’t afraid to call what has happened in Xinjiang a genocide.

Last fall, in the context of El-Sayed explaining why he called what Israel has done in recent years a genocide, Chuck Todd asked him if he considers what China is doing to the Uyghurs to be in the same category. His answer: “Yes. And the reason we don’t is because China is massively powerful and they swing their weight around to make sure we don’t use that word. Which is exactly why we should…it is our responsibility as people with some modicum of power to use it. Now the reason that a lot of people don’t is that you are often talking about far more powerful actors, and there may be a cost.”

But what should America do with that? Apparently, not much. On his policy platform, he declares that “I oppose the warlike pathway that the foreign policy establishment has pursued with China. Our competition with China is not fated toward kinetic war.” I couldn’t find him expanding on this thought anywhere online.

He then goes on to bring some vintage Jake Sullivan cooperate/compete energy:

Where we compete, it should be with our research, development, and economic power, building solutions to the problems of the future. While we must insist that China play by the rules when it comes to trade and intellectual property, we must also recognize that our shared futures are better when we cooperate with each other for the benefit of all of our people, rather than compete in a zero-sum arms race that makes all of us less safe.

We have maintained a policy of ‘strategic ambiguity’ with China on the question of Taiwan for decades. The future of Taiwan should be a matter for the Taiwanese to choose through democratic means. But in recognition of the possible risks, we must continue to onshore critical national security assets, such as chip manufacturing.

On AI, El-Sayed said last week with Ross Douthat that he was in favor of a “full on pause.” When Ross came back asking, “What happens if we pause and China doesn’t?” El-Sayed responded with the following:

El-Sayed: I don’t take that as seriously as a lot of people do. Here’s why: a lot of the frontier research is just spoofing our models. It would be like you’re pulling a skier on a boat, and you speed up the boat and say ‘oh the skier is still so close, we have to speed up!’ Well it’s because you’re pulling the skier. I think that’s in part what’s happening. They’ve been very good at mocking our technology. I think if we slow down, I think we’ll find that a lot of what China is doing is more about the dispersion of this technology than it is on frontier research.

And at the same time, I think we need an international treaty. We need to work with China…

Ross: Eventually the water skier can still swim and catch up…

El-Sayed: Yes the analogy breaks down… eventually they’ll be able to hop on a jetski and catch up. I think all of us are interested in the preservation of humanity. In China there are humans too and we’re humans too and creating robots to get to this point of recursive self improvement like that horror point in Fantasia where you’ve got the mops with the buckets that are self-creating…none of us want to get there and none of us what to see what happens when you open Pandora’s Box and all of a sudden AI has far exceeded our control. We all have an incentive to get this right and understand that we’re going to figure out how to work together similarly when it came to other potentially humanity-risking technological endeavours like nuclear power to be able to contain the potential threat and work together to make sure that we are focused more on protecting humanity than simply what the micro scale incentives might look like.

Good on the senator-elect for picking this analogy up from ten-time ChinaTalk guest Matt Sheehan’s Ezra appearance!

I’m impressed he’s digested the memes about distillation and diffusion in China, though I am a little surprised that we still have this “China can’t innovate” idea in our discourse around technology in 2026. On the diffusion question, he may get a kick out of our interview with Jeff Ding on the topic, while this piece by Nathan Lambert is a great distillation primer. Distillation helps Chinese labs catch up, but that doesn’t mean their own research stops when the American “boat” does.

El-Sayed is also a fan of export controls and broader AI regulation, calling for in his platform “compute controls, including ‘know your customer’ requirements for compute providers; and the creation of an independent technical agency with real enforcement power, like to the Food & Drug Administration, for AI.”

As senator from Michigan, he is unsurprisingly not enthusiastic about the idea of Chinese EV firms setting up shop in America. When Trump raised a trial balloon this fall he called this policy a “huge capitulation.” Instead, he wants an industrial policy that “makes sense,” one that targets “a $25,000, 300-mile range EV over the next seven years” (Will BYD be onto $25,000 flying cars by then?). He continued, “We should subsidize so that we can do that off the top in the next two years, and then slowly pull those subsidies. And as we do that, we should be tariffing the EV market so that we can use our own market to incubate that product, so that we can sell it on the global market and compete with Chinese low-cost EVs.”

He also alluded to disagreeing with Hasan Piker “on China” in a New Yorker interview. Perhaps El-Sayed doesn’t agree with Hasan that “China did [Tibet] a favor” by taking them over, that “Mao is one of the great leaders in the world,” who he would “never make fun of” and that China is the model of socialism the left should be looking toward.

James Talarico (D) — TX

Aqib: Talarico’s campaign was scant on China details with the exception of a general denouncement of tariffs and interest in protecting Uyghurs, but his voting record in the state legislature reveals a tiny bit more. Talarico opposed SB 17, which prevented Chinese citizens from acquiring Texas real estate. This led to Paxton’s campaign calling Talarico soft on China. Talarico defended his vote by arguing that the bill’s language was too broad and could restrict the actions of law-abiding legal immigrants. (SB17 did not restrict the activities of naturalized citizens or green-card holders.) Talarico similarly opposed SB 667, which mandated Texas state divestment from Chinese firms affiliated with Chinese intelligence agencies.

Talarico’s most hawkish tendencies stem from his position on AI and other technology, as he hopes to pass legislation to “enforce and strengthen export controls to keep advanced AI chips” away from China and other adversaries. While Talarico can definitely not be considered a “China Hawk,” we can expect him to be interested in technology competition against China.

Adam Hamilton (D) — KS

Disclosure: ChinaTalk’s Lily Ottinger, a Kansas native, has been volunteering for Adam Hamilton’s campaign this cycle.

Lily: Kansans have chosen Adam Hamilton to represent them in the US Senate, making him the first Democrat in 94 years to win that honor. He spent his career as a pastor building the largest United Methodist congregation in America, the 23,000-member Church of the Resurrection.

Senator-elect Hamilton has refrained from saying much about China during his whirlwind campaign — though his opponent, the Trump-loyalist incumbent Roger Marshall, told the audience of the Kansas State Fair debate that, “China loves this guy. China absolutely loves him.”

The only time Hamilton mentioned China during that debate makes me think that he’d enjoy subscribing to ChinaTalk [emphasis mine]:

“Well, last year, when you [Senator Roger Marshall] voted for the one big, beautiful bill, you gave $30 billion in tax cuts to data centers [...] across the country. So which is it: a moratorium or tax cuts for them?

So when it comes to AI, this is true. We have got to take seriously this potential threat. AI has wonderful potential, but also some devastating potential consequences. And you’ve been in office now for six years, and I’m just wondering why are we finally just getting around to talking about this? This is a very serious issue. We got to be concerned about it, we got to create the appropriate guardrails.

But at the same time, we can’t leave this alone. Russians and China, the Chinese are going to be working on this. As Americans, we have to do the same. So we got to be working on it, and at the same time we have appropriate guardrails. I think maybe this is one place where we both agree.”

China came up briefly in an interview with the Kansas Corn Growers Association in late October:

“We have also fallen horribly behind as the leading sponsors of public agricultural research. China spends vastly more resources on agricultural innovation. Our chief competitor in agriculture, Brazil, has nearly caught up with us. Our land-grant universities are home to remarkable agricultural scientists. With our help, their research can support further breakthroughs in agriculture—not only for production, but uses that add value to ag products.”

But as far as China policy goes, Senator-elect Hamilton has not said much… which is exactly why he should come on the ChinaTalk podcast!

Adam Hamilton, we would truly be honored to host you. We are a non-partisan publication, and, in the spirit of leading from the middle, we’ve interviewed plenty of Republicans from Capitol Hill too. Your team knows where to find me!

Kansas City at dusk. Doug Wertman/Wikimedia Commons.

Andy Barr (R) — KY

Jordan: Andy Barr, a 53-year-old veteran of the House since 2013 who will be taking Mitch McConnell’s seat, has a strong record passing China hawk legislation. In recent hearings, he pushed Secretary Rubio on delays to arms sales to Taiwan. Two years ago, he visited the island and told Townhall that “defending Taiwan is squarely within the national security interest of the United States.”

He was one of two votes out of committee against AI Overwatch (it passed 42-2-1). This bill would ban Blackwell exports to China. He did not explain his reasoning during markup. He also worked to pass a less stringent version of China outbound investment screening which would have imposed sanctions specifically on military and surveillance-linked firms instead of Cornyn’s bill that went after whole sectors. Recent Trump moves out of Treasury have aligned far more with Cornyn’s vision.

Julia Letlow (R) — LA

Aqib: Julia Letlow, the Senator-elect from Aqib’s home state of Louisiana, can easily be categorized as a China Hawk. Her Congressional website demonstrates concern over CCP influence in the Pacific, and her voting record as a US House Representative aligns with a “tough on China” stance. She voted in favor of TikTok divestment, decoupling from Chinese biotech firms like Wuxi, promoting Tibetan autonomy, protecting Uyghurs, and — of course — the Stop Chinese Fentanyl Act.

Her China Hawk stance also relates to her Louisiana constituency, especially as it pertains to Louisiana farmers and the state’s seafood industry. (Many Louisiana restaurants are shamed for using Chinese shellfish instead of Louisiana seafood, and protecting the state’s industry from cheaper Chinese imports is a salient concern.) Letlow advocated for decoupling from CCP-affiliated petroleum imports and land ownership in the US, called for a Section 301 investigation into unfair trade practices relating to seafood (a move lauded by the Southern Shrimp Alliance), and introduced the Safer Shrimp Imports Act.

We can ultimately expect a predictable pattern from Letlow, as we have her voting record as a Representative to envision her future record as a Senator. Letlow will be taking the seat of Senator Bill Cassidy (R), another China Hawk.

Kevin Hern (R) — OK

Lily: Prior to winning his Senate race, Kevin Hern represented Oklahoma’s 1st district in the US House of Representatives. In that role, he chaired the committee that introduced H.R. 7476, a bill that would, among other things, prohibit Chinese citizens from receiving federal grants for STEM research, ban Chinese EV batteries on American military bases, and give the president the power to sanction senior CCP officials for “threats or actions undermining the sovereignty of Taiwan[.]”

In an interview about the bill with the Hudson Institute, then-Representative Hern said:

“I don’t hate China, I just love America”

“[W]hat we’ve seen with Russian oil and energy coming to Europe and how that’s decimated our energy supply, we can’t allow that to happen when China ultimately invades Taiwan and does for chip production.”

As a Representative, Hern acknowledged the cost of tariffs on China in 2019, but he went on to offer resounding praise for Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs in 2025.

Trump won Oklahoma by +34.3 percentage points in 2024, while Hern won his 2026 Senate seat by +18.1 points. That represents a 16.2+ percentage point shift toward the Democrats, and compared to the four US House races Hern has won since 2018, 2026 is his narrowest-ever margin of victory. These numbers could make the senator-elect more hesitant to uncritically align with Trump’s agenda over the next two years.

Chris Pappas (D) — NH

Irene: New Hampshire’s new senator-elect was elected to the state legislature upon graduating from university. He became Congressional representative for New Hampshire’s 1st district in 2019 and is currently serving his fourth term. At 46, he has spent more than two decades in public life.

Most interestingly for our purposes, he has been involved in the Taiwan issue ever since being elected to the House. In 2020, he signed a congressional letter to the World Health Organization (WHO) advocating for Taiwan’s unconditional inclusion as a World Health Assembly observer and participation in WHO technical meetings. A year later, he co-sponsored H.R.1145, which would have directed the secretary of state to develop a strategy to regain WHO observer status for Taiwan. The Senate version, S.812, was eventually signed into law.

Rather than supporting maximalist positions like recognizing Taiwan’s independence or rejecting Beijing’s position, Pappas has worked on practical — if unsuccessful — efforts to strengthen US-Taiwan ties. During the 117th Congress, he was an original co-sponsor of a bill that would have explored setting up US border customs pre-clearance facilities in Taiwan. He joined three other Taiwan-related bills after their introduction, related to cybersecurity cooperation, financial deterrence against Chinese leaders, and a tax agreement, respectively. None of them became law. He also co-launched three bills to try to rename the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in the United States (TECRO), Taiwan’s de facto embassy in DC, to the “Taiwan Representative Office.”

We don’t know why Chris Pappas is a Taiwan fan, unfortunately. No records indicate that he has ever visited either Taiwan or mainland China. He’s attended events at TECRO and his office has received pro-Taiwan lobbying outreach, but not to especially notable extents. The Pappas campaign did not reply to our request for comments.

Chris Pappas (first from right) at a dinner with fellow House members and Ambassador Hsiao Bi-khim, then-head of TECRO in DC (and now vice president of Taiwan), in 2022. Source.

Oh, and there’s this too:

Annie Andrews (D) — SC

Irene: Dr. Annie Andrews, a physician, has never held public office, so all our knowledge about her China positions are from the campaign trail.

China became a surprisingly salient issue in the South Carolina senate race because of Republican candidate Darline Graham’s husband, Larry Nordone. The Washington Post uncovered in October that Nordone worked for companies that imported from a Zhengzhou-based manufacturer with defense ties, despite his wife’s opposition to Chinese manufacturing. Andrews, then, seized on this opportunity to accuse Graham of “lining her pockets with money from China.”

Back in August, after her opponent Graham made another misstep by admitting on stage that she knew little about the South China Sea, Taiwan, or national security, Andrews mocked that at least two of her own children “know where Taiwan is on a map.” But her thinking on China goes a bit beyond cheap jabs. On CNN’s Laura Coates Live, she called China “an existential threat” and Taiwan “a courageous democracy.”

As an inexperienced new legislator from a small state, Andrews is unlikely to have influence over China policy. Her comments, however, indicate a hawkish inkling.

Juliana Stratton (D) — IL

Quinn: As Illinois’s lieutenant governor under JB Pritzker for two terms, Juliana Stratton cheered the Gotion battery plant, owned by a Chinese parent company, as “a game-changer” for the state. However, her China policy remained largely theoretical during her primary victory over former House China Committee Ranking Member Raja Krishnamoorthi in the primary and subsequent victory in the general election.

Our best evidence for her China policy comes from her response to a single Sun-Times questionnaire from February. Stratton argued that “Trump’s trade war with China isn’t working,” noting higher prices brought about by tariffs and China’s “record-breaking $1.2 trillion trade surplus.” In a rebuke to this administration’s policy of cutting off foreign supply without domestic investment, Stratton urged the pursuit of real industrial policy:

We should invest in American infrastructure, advanced technology, and workforce in order to compete with China. Attracting and retaining foreign businesses. Equipping our workforce with the tools they need to thrive in a 21st century economy.

Whether she and other Democrats can push this through an executive branch that prefers self-imposed industrial scarcity and ballrooms to meaningful supply chain security and infrastructure investment remains to be seen.

Yet she also toed a more hawkish line, arguing that “we cannot ignore China’s threats to our national security,” focusing on protecting “intellectual property and data against Chinese cybersecurity threats.” And in a pleasant reprisal to the Trump administration’s use of Taiwan as a bargaining chip, Stratton said that the US must bolster ties with Taiwan, “supporting its self-defense capabilities and helping to secure its semiconductor manufacturing and significant global supply chain implications.”

Peggy Flanagan (D) — MN

Quinn: The first Native American woman ever elected to the US Senate, Peggy Flanagan campaigned on a similar platform to other progressive candidates, more so emphasizing economic security at the individual level than at the national level. However, like other midwestern Democrats, she also focused on steel and farms.

A foil to the Trumpist “all tariffs are good tariffs” line of thought, Flanagan sought to distinguish between protectionist tariffs designed to protect American industry and vindictive tariffs that needlessly raise prices for American consumers. As she said in a recent debate, “steel tariffs in particular are important, but the tariffs that we see happening right now… are killing… our industries.” However, at the FarmFest debate, while her opponents were quick to mention China with respect to soybeans and CCP-owned American farmland, Flanagan did not bring up China a single time.

Flanagan seems to be remarkably AGI-pilled for a congressperson, calling AI “an existential threat” and has backed safeguards and shutdown capability, while faulting the fact that AI is moving at the pace of corporate interests. In response to this and news of donations from employees at AI firms like Anthropic, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) wrote a rambling tirade, which we excerpt here:

Peggy Flanagan is a socialist doomer who wants to kill innovation and give China the upper hand by pushing effective altruism dogma and fighting alongside the likes of Bernie Sanders to unleash crippling government regulations on artificial intelligence.

The NRSC also branded her a “a tool for the Chinese Communist Party” for accepting two $3,500 donations from Pin Ni 倪频, the head of a major U.S. subsidiary of China’s Wanxiang Group, which makes automotive parts. Ni notably also gave money to the RNC, which it happily accepted at the time.

For all the NRSC’s complaints, we would be remiss to not mention that arguing for AI safety is not the same thing as ceding the upper hand to China and may, in fact, actually help the AI race. Likewise, accepting campaign donations from the head of a company that has saved thousands of jobs in your state and invested heavily in manufacturing in the Midwest seems rather milquetoast in the context of the Trump administration’s preferred forms of corruption.

Scott Colom

We didn’t turn up Mississippi’s Scott Colom mentioning China directly on the campaign trail, though he did frame the problem with the tariff war as something hurting Mississippi’s soybean farmers. A PAC who bought ads in Mississippi did run this (pretty offensive) attack ad.

Andrew Solender

Harriet Hageman (R) — WY

Senator-elect Hageman’s China stance can also be largely deduced from her track record in the House. She can generally be categorized as a China Hawk given her commitment to counter the “latent aggression and malign influence” of the country. Her main interest in China competition likely stems from an energy and critical minerals perspective, two areas in which her state has a vested interest.

She has traveled to Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea for pursuing greater partnership on energy security, and she has been vocal and seemingly well versed in the critical minerals competition. She is worried about China’s control of critical minerals processing, and she wants to make it easier for American companies to develop rare earths projects in Wyoming like the Brook Mine and Halleck Creek. When it comes to critical minerals competition, Hageman is more interested in permitting reform to make building in America easier and less interested in issues like a green transition, given Wyoming’s oil and gas industry.

We can expect Senator Hageman to vote broadly with the China Hawk coalition when it comes to national security topics and be especially proactive about energy and minerals competition.

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

SPACEXSI

📞 SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot starts making phone calls

Image source: SpaceXSI

The Rundown: SpaceXSI just rolled out phone calls in Grok Bot, the company’s AI agent platform, which can now sit on hold, book appointments, and negotiate bills on U.S. numbers — with users legally responsible for every call the bot makes.

The details:

If a rep asks something the bot can’t answer, users get a message mid-call and type a reply for it to pass along, all while following a live transcript.

SpaceXSI’s terms make users the “caller of record,” “solely responsible” for calls and for following phone laws, with bots disclosing they’re a “virtual assistant.”

The calls appear to run directly inside the platform via a temporary number, with early examples including a Comcast bill negotiation and a pizza order.

Grok Bot is available for paid users, and Elon Musk answered complaints about usage limits by calling the platform’s cost “unsustainably high relative to revenue.”

Why it matters: AI labs keep pitching agents as a way to take annoying life tasks off people’s plates, and for many, phone calls sit near the top of that list. With Grok Voice already answering 20,000 Starlink calls a day by SpaceXSI’s own count, the phone could soon go the way of the agentic internet — bots talking with other bots.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

🗺️ Nate’s Notebook: Make AI sketch before it builds

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: TED grew on two ideas. Make the world’s best and brightest distill their biggest idea into 18 minutes or less. Then help them with the visuals, because communicating complicated ideas with strong visuals takes a separate level of genius altogether. Nancy Duarte’s design team helped speakers rework their slides.

If you’re on a $20 AI plan, you’ve probably had a few aha moments and started running out of credits. You also have an entire graphic design department sitting in that chat. Claude’s custom visuals and ChatGPT’s new Intelligent UI can drop a chart, table, or flow diagram right into the reply.

Every session is finite, expiring intelligence. The question is where to thrash. Most people thrash way too late, trying to make huge swinging changes to a deck or website that’s already built. They burn their tokens, run out of credits, and still end up frustrated. You can’t change where the Mississippi River exits in Louisiana; you’ve got to change the trickle up top.

So before anything gets built, I tell it: don’t start yet. This is where we’re eventually going, but conserve your energy until we agree on the path. Never give me more than a paragraph or two. Ask me smart multiple-choice questions, or better yet, sketch it right in the chat, so you can cut big chunks of work you’ll never have to do.

AI TRAINING

🆓 Which free AI tool should you actually use?

The Rundown: ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity all have free plans. But they offer different tools and limits. In this guide, you’ll run the same tasks in each one, check the results, and build a small AI toolkit without paying for the six.

Step-by-step:

Open the six services and check that each account is on its free plan. Use personal accounts and keep private work out of the test

Paste the same fictional Repair Café brief into each assistant (all resources in the full guide). Check the event time, staffing, budget, and missing details

Ask each tool the same question about Shenandoah National Park. Open the official National Park Service source and check the leash rule and trail restrictions

Upload the same small budget CSV wherever the free tier allows it. If uploads are unavailable, paste the data and record that limit separately

Score each result for accuracy, source quality, file handling, and usefulness. Choose a main assistant, a research tool, and a backup based on results

Pro tip: A free plan can be generous for chat but tight on uploads, image creation, or research. Check the limit that applies to the task you actually do.

AI & THE MIDTERMS

⛔️ Midterm voters turn on data centers, AI

Image source: datacentersontheballot.com

The Rundown: Voters in U.S. midterms backed limits on data centers almost everywhere those measures appeared on local ballots and handed Congress to Democrats, promising tougher oversight of Silicon Valley, with a majority also telling NBC they expect AI to do more harm than good.

The details:

Data center opponents have taken 38 of 39 fully counted local measures, according to election trackers, with only Harwood, N.D., voting the other way.

In NBC’s exit poll, 76% of voters would oppose a data center going up in their own community, and 57% expect AI to hurt society more than help.

Goldman Sachs reportedly sees 45% of planned U.S. data center capacity at risk of temporary freezes, but figures the political heat will cool over time.

Elon Musk, the biggest midterm donor at $446M backing Republicans, posted that data centers in space look “pretty appealing right now,” following the results.

Why it matters: The public has heavily rebuked AI and the data center buildout in the midterms. With AI infrastructure hubs like Texas flipping blue and Democrats about to run the hearings on AI regulation, the ground under the entire industry just shifted — and the days of a hands-off federal approach to U.S. AI labs are likely coming to an end.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Keith built an AI archive of handwritten 1940s family letters

Today’s workflow comes from reader Keith Weinberger:

“I built a family archive website to host handwritten letters and photos from a relative’s 1942/43 stint in basic training. I built everything through prompts, and it could help anyone with scanned family papers who wants them searchable and open to AI chat.

I designed the basic website in Google AI Studio. I migrated the project to Replit for the build-out and hosting. I used Firebase for PDF and photo storage, and a Firebase database for users and data indexing.

I built a PDF upload workflow that extracts text from the handwritten letters. I chunk the PDFs for faster retrieval, since the files are large. The workflow creates a search index and a vector database for AI chat. I created server APIs to retrieve data and content, which avoids CORS issues. The result is a site where the letters and photos can be searched and queried through AI chat.”

EXPERT COMMENTARY

After a momentous US election, it’s still shaky ground for American democracy

By J. Scott Marcus

READ MORE

The repudiation of Donald Trump and his enablers in the midterms is absolutely stunning in its breadth and scope. It exceeds even the most optimistic polling results.

The results and projections in the early hours of 4 November indicated that the Democrats had pretty much ‘run the table’ on the Senate races they hoped to win, including states where a Democratic victory in a normal year would have been almost unthinkable – Texas, Kansas and Iowa, even winning a surprise victory in South Carolina.

The Democrats have won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, a result that only a few months ago would have been seen as exceedingly unlikely.

IRAN. Looking down the barrel

Tehran isn’t ready to concede, and neither is Trump.

Brent crude fell 8% amid speculation Donald Trump would fire Pete Hegseth and the Democrats would withhold war powers in Congress. Tehran said four tankers caught fire hitting mines in Hormuz as it held a mock execution of Trump.

INTELLIGENCE. As in other areas, Trump has never sought Congress’s permission, and he can always fund the war from existing budgets. It also takes two to TACO. Even if he wanted to end the war, Iran won’t let him without harsh terms. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the US’s collapse had accelerated and “the slightest inclination toward submission” would only embolden it, adding that US enmity would persist regardless of who was in power.

FOR BUSINESS. Trump’s strategic choices remain what they were at the start of the week – escalation or capitulation – even if the politics have changed. And while Tuesday’s result was met in tones conciliatory by Trump’s standards, he still has enough pride to defend the war and deny he’s sacking Hegseth (who may nonetheless take a Senate vacancy). Likewise, he won’t want to follow a 1974-level drubbing with a 1975-style evacuation from a foreign theatre.

UNITED STATES. Water off a lame duck's back

It is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.

The White House posted a “public service announcement” that Trump was still president after the media reported his administration’s “death knell” and “the beginning of the end”. JD Vance told Twitter: “the reason we lost is the war.”...

November 05, 2026 | Listen online | Read online

Welcome, humans.

Okay, so apparently the fastest way to annoy a school district is to tell it, "Sure, you can turn off our AI, but then you lose Google Search." Bold strategy, Google.

That's roughly what happened Tuesday. Google told schools they could switch off Gemini, but switching off its other AI features would cost them Search, which now runs heavily on AI-generated answers. After the backlash, Google made Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search off by default, with schools turning each one on individually.

Enter DuckDuckGo, which posted instructions for switching a school's default search engine and accused Google of "forcing AI on school children." Turns out "ours has an off switch" is a pretty good sales pitch. One caveat: the privacy case is DuckDuckGo's own pitch, and TechCrunch doesn't detail what Google does with student data.

Here’s what happened in AI today:

📰 OpenAI agreed to acquire code-hosting startup Pierre Computer

📰 Meta acquired multi-agent coding startup Conductor

🍪 Moonshot released open weights for Kimi K3.1 Pro

🎓 AI agents booked just four Uber rides in Halloween week

OpenAI's New Image Models Make GIFs, Remember Your Characters, and Run 50% Faster

Ever asked ChatGPT for a logo, loved it, requested one tiny tweak, and gotten back a completely different logo? Same.

That “change one thing, change everything” problem is what OpenAI's new Images 2.6 is mostly built to fix. It's rolling out in ChatGPT (every subscription tier) and Codex (OpenAI's coding agent), and developers get the models through the API. OpenAI also says people make about 4 billion images a week across its products, roughly one for every two humans on Earth.

Here's what's new:

Speed: about 50% faster, per OpenAI. The API's speed-focused model can make an image in as little as six seconds at low quality, per early coverage.

GIFs: short animated loops from characters, mascots, product shots, sketches, or storyboards.

Saved references: store pictures of yourself, a pet, or a character once, then reuse them.

For developers: image markup, SVG export, and a new "complexity" setting.

The saved references are the part I'd test first. Image models usually don't remember your dog between requests, so keeping Biscuit looking like Biscuit across five scenes meant re-uploading him every time and hoping. Saved references skip that step, aiming for consistent characters, products, and brand details across edits.

Image markup comes to the API too. Instead of typing "shrink the logo on the sleeve, no, the OTHER sleeve," you mark the exact spot on the image. Finally, an end to "your left or my left."

SVG export saves a design as shapes stored as instructions (draw a curve from here to there) instead of a grid of pixels, so it stays sharp at any size and a designer can still edit it. We couldn't find how well it handles photo-like images, so try a logo first.

The complexity setting controls how much planning the model does before it draws. OpenAI recommends low for quick edits and medium or high for crowded scenes with lots of constraints. The two API models split the same tradeoff: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare is built for speed and layouts like posters, while GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst is built for more detail and consistent edits.

So here's the test: put one character in five different scenes, with a few edits in between. If scene five still looks like scene one, the pitch holds. If not, 50% faster doesn't help much when you're regenerating the same image three times.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Run the 50 Second Test Before You Automate

Uber just put a number on how much people trust agents with small chores. During Halloween week, its busiest week of October, AI agents booked only four rides and about 500 food orders, out of roughly 320 million total trips and orders. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called the traction "very, very early and very limited." He also pointed at a likely reason: booking a ride in the Uber app takes about 50 seconds, and reordering a favorite meal takes about 90. Turns out "just tell the robot" has to beat "tap, tap, done."

The hidden cost is delegation overhead: explaining the job, granting access, waiting, checking the result, and cleaning up when something goes wrong. If all that takes longer than doing the task yourself, the agent didn't save you time. It handed you a new job called supervising the agent. (Khosrowshahi still sees agents as a potential "net positive" for Uber's demand, so this is a snapshot of right now.)

Before you automate anything, run a quick break-even check:

Time one clean manual run, start to finish.

Estimate the one-time setup time, plus the review time you'll spend checking each automated run.

Divide setup time by the seconds saved per run (manual time minus review time). That's how many repetitions it takes to pay back.

Say a task takes 50 seconds by hand, setting up an agent takes 30 minutes, and you'd spend 20 seconds checking each result. You save 30 seconds a run, so it takes 60 runs to break even (1,800 seconds divided by 30). Do it twice a week and that's about 30 weeks. If review takes as long as the task itself, it never pays back.

Or hand the math to your chatbot:

Evaluate this workflow for automation: Manual time per run: [ ] Automation setup time: [ ] Review time per run: [ ] Runs per month: [ ] Calculate the break-even point, monthly time saved, and failure cost. Recommend automate, assist, or keep manual.

"Failure cost" is what it costs you when the agent gets it wrong, like the wrong ride or a double-ordered dinner. Aim at the first repetitive task where the savings still show up after setup, supervision, and the occasional failure.

Enlargement is getting real: Is the EU ready?

Enlargement is getting real: Is the EU ready?. Enlargement is getting real: Is the EU ready? marianna.liana… Thu, 11/05/2026 - 10:46 5 minutes It feels like EU enlargement is getting closer. The Commission is no longer just assessing whether enlargement partners are ready to join. It is proposing steps to prepare the EU to welcome them in. With its October Preparing for a Wider Union communication, the Commission has set out proposals to adapt the EU's decision-making, policies and budget to accommodate new members. The 2026 Enlargement Package thus comes at a time when the prospect of the next enlargement is beginning to take a somewhat more concrete shape. Yet the path to membership looks different for each enlargement partner. For some, the task is to sustain reform progress and bring negotiations to a close. For others, it is to translate progress in negotiations into lasting reforms, overcome political deadlock or reverse democratic backsliding. The Commission's new indicative roadmaps for Albania, Moldova, Montenegro and Ukraine set out milestones for the year ahead, offering a more concrete framework for the next steps. Yet their focus on the coming year, rather than firm deadlines for concluding negotiations, also illustrates the limits of the predictability they can offer. For the EU, the challenge is to move from preparing for enlargement to making the decisions that will enable it: adapting its institutions and policies, ensuring that reform progress is rewarded, and securing the political support needed to see enlargement through. Turning momentum into membership Montenegro and Moldova are at different stages of accession, but both raise the question of what it will take to translate negotiating progress into membership. Having provisionally closed 21 of its 33 chapters, including 14 during the latest reporting period, Podgorica has entered the final stage of accession negotiations. Work on the country’s accession treaty is underway. Sustaining cross-party cooperation, addressing outstanding issues raised by Croatia in the spirit of good neighbourly relations, and implementing judicial and anti-corruption reforms will be essential to bringing negotiations to a close. Chisinau faces a different test: sustaining rapid progress while building the capacity to meet the obligations of membership. Reforms have advanced, including in the judiciary, despite sustained Russian interference and the growing security repercussions of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Maintaining momentum will require stronger public administration and effective implementation of institutional reforms. While Montenegro must demonstrate its readiness to conclude negotiations, Moldova must show that its institutions can keep pace with the accession process. Turning progress into lasting reforms For Albania and Ukraine, advances in accession negotiations need to be accompanied by sustained reforms, particularly in the rule of law. In Albania, large.

Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece

Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece. Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama Revisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong , is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism. Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film. Continue reading.

AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the E.U.’s New Rules

AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the E.U.’s New Rules. The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on Open AI’s new text Grain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new E.U. law , show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether text Grain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated. AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next “tokens” (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li , coauthor of the text Grain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words. A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values—numbers produced by a mathematical process that influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says. What makes text Grain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and text Grain adjusts to that target. This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money.… In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.” Limits of AI Watermark Detection The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written. Open AI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. In tests on psychology questions from the ELI5 database , which gathers questions and answers from the r/explainlikeimfive subreddit, the model detected watermarks in about 80 percent of 200-token text ( approximately 150 words ) compared to 95 percent of 400-token text (approximately 300 words). Li says this is a “basic limitation” of text-watermarking technologies and would be complicated to solve. Short passages may not contain enough watermark evidence for reliable detection, even with additional computation, he adds, while longer passages generally provide more. Editing also weakens the signal. In an evaluation of.

Democrats’ midterm gains put US data centre boom under pressure

Democrats’ midterm gains put US data centre boom under pressure. The AI industry's biggest building boom now sits largely under US Democratic leadership, with incoming governors promising tougher restrictions and voters widely signalling approval of data centre measures offered to them in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats flipped five governorships in Tuesday's elections: Texas , Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada. Together, those states hold 37 per cent of planned data centre capacity in the US, according to our analysis of data from Cleanview, which tracks data centre projects and capacity. Texas accounts for the biggest share, with 22.8 per cent of planned US capacity. Its incoming governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, has promised a moratorium on their construction and greater community input into where data centres are built. The incoming governors of Georgia and Ohio, Keisha Lance Bottoms and Amy Acton, have also pledged pauses on construction of large data centres. This matters because governors have considerable influence over where and how data centres are built. They appoint utility regulators who oversee electricity prices and grid connections, and have a say over the tax incentives used to attract investment. They also shape state-level infrastructure and development policy, although local authorities retain important planning powers. Democrats also flipped seven Senate seats in states holding 32 per cent of planned data centre capacity. As The National reported this week , control of Congress gives Democrats more oversight of the AI sector. However, analysts expect gridlock rather than sweeping change while President Donald Trump retains veto power. Georgetown University’s Mark Mc Carthy said the new Congress was more likely to protect households from paying for data centres’ power costs. Data centres on the ballot The backlash we charted before the vote also reached the ballot directly. Voters in 38 local jurisdictions across 10 states considered at least 41 data centre measures, Reuters reported, citing Ballotpedia. Ohio had the most, with 21 proposals. Voters approved nearly every moratorium on the ballot. Big issue, but not the main issue Of course, data centres alone did not decide the elections. Among the biggest issues for voters were the cost of living, groceries and health care. But the data centre debate is increasingly tied to those concerns, particularly over rising electricity bills and who ultimately pays for the infrastructure needed to support the AI boom. The results point to a national wave of data centre scepticism in political office. That matters for an industry in a race to build. For tech investors, the bigger questions may be what new governors in states such as Texas will do next. The building boom has continued this year despite growing opposition. Crucifer Academy turns kids into teachers with a new AI tool

Crucifer Academy turns kids into teachers with a new AI tool. The Knowledge Guarantee, Crucifer Academy’s integrated training and lab methodology, moves away from traditional training methods to ensure that learning is actually taking place. While conventional training involves memorising and recalling data, the Knowledge Guarantee ensures comprehension of the underlying principles and logic behind that data. Completion is based on demonstrated understanding as opposed to attendance alone. But how does it work? . At the centre of the model is the AI Kid, an interactive digital avatar that the learner must teach after a module. The AI Kid asks questions, challenges unclear explanations and asks for alternative ways to understand the concept. Once the student successfully teaches the avatar, the AI Kid itself takes the assessment to prove that the learner has mastered the material before moving forward. The avatar is designed to answer on the basis of what the learner taught it. This methodology goes beyond adding an AI character to an online course, as Crucifer aims to give employers clearer proof of what a learner understands and ultimately change what it means to say that someone has learned. Mastery over milestones The Dubai-based academy, part of Crucifer AI Technologies, is preparing to welcome its first cohort with an approach that challenges the conventional pace of education. Its philosophy is simple: the standard of learning should never be compromised, even if the time it takes to achieve it varies from one student to another. Although designed as a six-month programme, the course allows learners to take nine or even 12 months if they need more time to master the material. Additional teaching, repeat sessions and one-to-one support come without further tuition fees. Rather than measuring success by how quickly learners completes the programme, the emphasis is on what they have genuinely learned and can demonstrate. This is what the academy means by its learning guarantee. It is a commitment to supporting each student until each student's understanding has been assessed and verified, rather than a promise of employment at the end of the course. The approach also places a different kind of responsibility on the academy itself. Enrolment is not simply a matter of paying the fees, and the provider absorbs the cost of any additional teaching required. An initial assessment of each applicant's capacity to learn helps establish the foundations for a model in which the institution is as accountable for the learning experience as the student is for their own progress. “We are not asking employers to trust that someone attended a course,” says Christopher Richard, founder of Crucifer AI Technologies. “We are building a model in which the learner must repeatedly show that they understand, can apply what they know and can explain their decisions.” Potential outweighs credentials The approach begins before the first lesson, with an admission.

The midterm elections’ blue wave could throw a wrench in Space X’s mobile ambitions. Elon Musk has made no secret of his hopes of turning Space X into a viable competitor to mobile companies like Verizon and AT&T. But with the Democrats’ resounding victory in the 2026 midterm elections, that plan is suddenly thrown into question. Space X has been busy over the past month making deals and positioning itself to step into the mobile space. In October, it bought an 800 MHz spectrum portfolio from private equity firm Grain Management, which had acquired it from T-Mobile following its 2020 merger with Sprint. And earlier this week, Space X struck a deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its planned mobile carrier. Taken together, those moves bring the company closer to entering the market. But to launch the new division, Space X will also have to jump through legislative hoops, something that could be significantly more challenging with the Democrats in charge. Several Democratic candidates made it clear they planned to target Musk —who spent $500 million trying to stop the blue wave —should the party gain a majority in the midterms. The midterm elections’ biggest loser? Data centers

The midterm elections’ biggest loser? Data centers. Data centers were on the ballot this election, and they lost. While results from the midterm elections are still coming in, as of November 4, 38 out of 39 restrictions on data centers had passed—from temporary moratoriums on new construction to full bans. And multiple candidates who made opposition to data centers a key part of their campaign also won. Take the example of William Lawrence , the Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan’s purple 7 th Congressional District, which Trump narrowly won in 2024. Lawrence, a progressive community organizer and cofounder of the Sunrise Movement , was new to politics and faced a challenge running against the Trump-backed incumbent, Tom Barrett. In the primary, facing two establishment Democrats who had raised more money, Lawrence won in part because he vowed to fight data centers. “He found an issue that connected with local residents across partisanship,” says Matt Grossman, director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University. Recent polls say that seven in 10 Americans don’t want data centers to be built in their communities, for reasons ranging from potential impacts on electric bills to noise and water use. William Lawrence , a Democratic congressional candidate in Michigan, speaks at his election night event in Lansing. He defeated a Republican opponent. [Photo: Bill Pugliano/Getty Images] In his first ad , Lawrence stood at a farm and said, “Tech billionaires want to turn this field into a massive data center that’ll jack up our energy bills and ruin our home values.” After going to local planning meetings to watch data center developers pitch projects, he said that it was an “abuse of power” in communities that didn’t have the resources to fight back. He also called for other controls on technology, including a pause on development of advanced artificial intelligence and mandatory safety requirements for AI. Barrett, his Republican opponent, had supported data centers in the past That included a vote for a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that would have stopped states’ ability to regulate AI , and likely also data centers, for a decade. (The provision was later taken out of the bill). The OBBBA includes tax breaks for companies building out AI infrastructure. Barrett also voted for the SPEED Act, which accelerates data center construction As backlash to data centers grew, Barrett argued that communities should have local control over whether projects get built, but the message fell flat. Lawrence won. Barrett was unpopular for other reasons—including the fact that he’d never held a local town hall—and it’s not clear that data centers were the thing that made voters push him out, versus anger about the Iran war, tariffs’ impact on the Michigan economy, and other factors. It’s probably too early to say that data centers as an issue swung a race, says Daniel Schi.
